chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:27:Mutations such as D614G, observed in nearly all modern SARS-CoV-2 sequences, reflect genuine fitness advantages, but the rate of near-fixation is amplified by founder effects during the early pandemic, making it difficult to distinguish the relative contributions of selection and genetic drift from frequency data alone.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:31:Mullick et al.~\cite{mullick2021entropy} combined Shannon entropy with K-means clustering to detect hotspots in the SARS-CoV-2 Spike protein.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:34:Large-scale frequency-based analyses have been applied to SARS-CoV-2~\cite{koyama2020variant,obermeyer2022analysis}, but these studies used single information types (mutation frequency or fitness proxies) without systematic comparison against alternative scoring approaches.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:43:An important limitation of frequency-based mutation analysis is \textbf{phylogenetic non-in\-de\-pen\-dence}: mutations observed in closely related sequences are not independent events~\cite{felsenstein1985phylogenies}.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:74:direct application to the SARS-CoV-2 genome with default parameters results in 99.76\% of the data being merged into a single massive cluster; even with manually tuned parameters ($\varepsilon = 0.15$, MinPts $= 5$), only 4 undifferentiated clusters are obtained, rendering biologically meaningful hotspot distinction impossible~\cite{youn2025mutclust}.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:103:Starr et al.~\cite{starr2020dms} measured ACE2 binding affinity and protein expression for all single amino acid substitutions in the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD), revealing that most RBD positions are highly constrained for binding.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:105:Lee et al.~\cite{lee2018h3n2dms} performed DMS of influenza H3N2 hemagglutinin (HA), demonstrating that DMS fitness measurements can predict the evolutionary fates of naturally circulating variants.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:106:Bloom and Neher~\cite{bloom2023fitness} provided an integrated analysis of DMS fitness effects across all SARS-CoV-2 proteins, establishing a comprehensive reference for the entire viral proteome.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:112:Finally, DMS coverage across the viral world remains sparse: the EVEREST benchmark~\cite{gurev2025everest} catalogued only 45 DMS datasets across all WHO priority viruses, and comprehensive DMS data exist for fewer than 20 viral proteins.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:146:Beyond single-model predictions, \textbf{EVEscape}~\cite{thadani2023evescape} demonstrated the value of combining PLM-derived features with complementary biological information.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:147:EVEscape integrates three components to predict viral immune escape mutations: (1)~EVE fitness scores from a Bayesian variational autoencoder trained on MSAs, (2)~structural accessibility from experimentally determined structures (PDB) or AlphaFold predictions, and (3)~physicochemical dissimilarity between wildtype and mutant residues (charge and hydrophobicity changes).
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:148:Its success in forecasting SARS-CoV-2 Omicron escape mutations from pre-pandemic data illustrates the potential of multi-source feature integration.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:150:\textbf{AlphaMissense}~\cite{cheng2023alphamissense} adopted an AlphaFold-derived architecture to classify missense variants across the entire human proteome, achieving high accuracy for pathogenicity prediction.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:151:However, its training data and evaluation are centered on human genetic variants, and the distinct evolutionary dynamics of viral proteins---rapid evolution, high mutation rates, and population-level rather than individual-level selection---limit the direct applicability of AlphaMissense to viral variant effect prediction.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:154:The EVEREST benchmark~\cite{gurev2025everest} found that PLMs substantially underperform alignment-based methods on viral proteins, suggesting that the evolutionary patterns learned from predominantly cellular organism sequences may not transfer well to fast-evolving viral proteins.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:159:The most comprehensive benchmark for PLM-based variant effect prediction is ProteinGym~\cite{notin2023proteingym}, which evaluates over 70 predictors on 217 DMS assays spanning 2.7 million substitution variants, primarily from human and model organism proteins.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:160:ProteinGym has been instrumental in establishing performance rankings among PLMs and alignment-based methods for the per-mutation fitness prediction task: given a specific amino acid substitution at a specific position, predict its continuous fitness effect (evaluated by Spearman correlation against DMS measurements).
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:161:MutBench differs from ProteinGym in three fundamental respects.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:162:First, the \textit{task} differs: ProteinGym evaluates per-mutation effect prediction (a continuous regression problem), whereas MutBench evaluates per-region hotspot detection (a binary classification problem over genomic regions).
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:163:Second, the \textit{domain} differs: ProteinGym focuses on human and model organism proteins, while MutBench targets viral proteins across 11 pathogens with distinct evolutionary dynamics.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:164:Third, the \textit{analysis objective} differs: ProteinGym ranks prediction methods, while MutBench quantifies the scoring--pathogen interaction to determine which biological information source is optimal for each virus.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:165:These distinctions make ProteinGym and MutBench complementary rather than competing: ProteinGym establishes which PLMs best predict individual mutation effects, while MutBench establishes which information types (including but not limited to PLM-derived scores) best identify mutation-enriched genomic regions across diverse pathogens.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:172:\textbf{Nextstrain}~\cite{nextstrain2018hadfield} integrates phylogenetic analysis with geographic and temporal metadata to track pathogen evolution in real time. Its primary function is to answer ``which lineages are currently spreading and where?''---for example, tracking the geographic expansion of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron sublineages or seasonal influenza clades. Nextstrain visualizes the evolutionary relationships among circulating variants but does not evaluate or compare methods for detecting mutation-prone positions.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:174:\textbf{PANGO}~\cite{rambaut2020pangolin} provides a standardized lineage classification system for SARS-CoV-2, assigning labels (e.g., BA.2.86, JN.1) to sequences based on their phylogenetic placement. Its purpose is taxonomic organization---labeling ``what is this variant?''---rather than identifying which genomic positions are likely to accumulate future mutations of functional significance.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:192:Maher et al.~\cite{maher2022predicting} analyzed a comprehensive set of features predicting future SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern, including mutation frequency, phylogenetic placement, geographic spread, growth rate, and structural properties.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:194:However, their analysis was restricted to SARS-CoV-2, and the feature importance hierarchy they established may not generalize to pathogens with different evolutionary dynamics.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:196:Rodriguez-Rivas et al.~\cite{rodriguez2022epistatic} took a co-evolutionary approach, applying Direct Coupling Analysis (DCA) to model epistatic interactions between positions in SARS-CoV-2 proteins.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:198:This result highlights that mutual information between positions---capturing the constraint network within protein structures---provides predictive power beyond what single-position features can offer. The broader DCA / EVcouplings / GREMLIN family of position-coupling methods is intentionally outside the 20-scoring panel of MutBench (Section~\ref{sec:scoring_detection}), which restricts itself to single-position scorers to enable the orthogonal scoring~$\times$~detection-family ANOVA decomposition; epistasis-aware extensions are flagged as future work in Chapter~\ref{ch:discussion}.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:203:EVEscape~\cite{thadani2023evescape} demonstrated that combining evolutionary fitness predictions with structural accessibility and physicochemical dissimilarity features can predict viral escape mutations, providing a practical example of multi-source information integration for viral mutation analysis.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:206:A critical limitation shared by all these studies is their focus on \textbf{single pathogens}---primarily SARS-CoV-2 or influenza.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:208:This is the gap that the present study addresses: by evaluating 10 information types across 11 pathogens, MutBench quantifies the pathogen-specificity of feature importance and provides concrete recommendations for which information source to prioritize for each virus (Section~\ref{sec:information_analysis}).
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:226:Weber et al.~\cite{weber2019benchmarking} proposed guidelines for neutral benchmarking, articulating three core requirements: (1)~\textit{independent evaluation}, where the benchmark designer is distinct from the method developers; (2)~\textit{multiple metrics}, to capture different aspects of performance and avoid optimization for a single criterion; and (3)~\textit{controlled experimental design}, ensuring that all methods are evaluated on identical data under identical conditions. Mangul et al.~\cite{mangul2019systematic} extended these principles to a community-wide audit of omics computational tools, documenting systematic disparities in tool reliability that motivated the present study's emphasis on multi-pathogen rather than single-pathogen evaluation.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:236:(1)~ProteinGym~\cite{notin2023proteingym,notin2025proteingym_v13}, which benchmarks variant effect predictors using 217 DMS assays and 90+ baseline models (as of v1.3) but addresses a per-residue fitness-regression task rather than hotspot region detection;
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:237:(1b)~\textbf{ViroGym}~\cite{virogym2026} (Mar 2026), which benchmarks PLM and alignment-based scorers across 13 viruses, 79 DMS assays, 552{,}937 sequences, and 7 phenotypic categories including immune escape---larger virus count than MutBench, but focused on per-variant fitness rather than per-region detection;
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:240:and (4)~individual SARS-CoV-2 studies using entropy~\cite{harvey2021tracking} or clustering that validate against small variant sets without standardized ground truth.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:241:Among the 35+ mutation clustering tools catalogued in the computational oncology literature~\cite{pons2020computational}, none was designed for or validated on viral population-level mutation data. Cancer hotspot tools (OncodriveCLUSTL, HotMAPS, MutSpot) require tumor cohort somatic mutation calls and human-genome-specific background models (trinucleotide signatures, replication timing). Phylogenetic selection tools (MEME, FUBAR, FEL) detect per-codon dN/dS signals but do not perform spatial clustering of hotspot regions. The only virus-specific hotspot clustering tool is MutClust~\cite{youn2025mutclust}, validated on a single pathogen (SARS-CoV-2). This gap---the absence of systematic multi-pathogen hotspot detection benchmarking---is what MutBench addresses.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:246:Recent years have seen significant progress in benchmarking variant effect prediction (VEP) methods on proteins. ProteinGym~\cite{notin2023proteingym} established a large-scale benchmark comprising 217 DMS assays and 2.7 million substitution variants, primarily for human and model organism proteins. EVE~\cite{frazer2021eve}, a Bayesian VAE trained on evolutionary sequences, demonstrated that unsupervised generative models can predict disease-associated variants without clinical labels. EVEscape~\cite{thadani2023evescape} extended this framework to viral immune escape prediction by combining EVE fitness scores with structural accessibility and physicochemical dissimilarity, successfully forecasting SARS-CoV-2 Omicron escape mutations from pre-pandemic data.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:248:Most recently, EVEREST~\cite{gurev2025everest,gurev2026everest_v3} specifically benchmarked VEP methods across WHO priority viruses; the v3 expansion (Jan 2026) covers 45 viral DMS datasets, 31 forecasting clades across 4 viruses, and reliability assessment across 40 WHO priority RNA viruses spanning 16 viral families. EVEREST finds that protein language models substantially underperform alignment-based approaches on viral proteins, that reliability fails for over half of the WHO-40 panel (especially surface glycoproteins), and that prediction reliability varies dramatically across pathogens---a finding that independently corroborates the LOPO 0/11 non-transferability reported in MutBench Chapter~\ref{ch:results}.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:249:The PLANT framework~\cite{plant2025antigenic} and Shah et al.~\cite{shah2024h3n2ml} provide PLM-based and ML-based H3N2 antigenic cartography that explicitly competes with WHO vaccine-strain selection, building on the foundational antigenic-cartography paradigm of Smith et al.~\cite{smith2004antigenic}; MutBench's H3N2 self-consistency check (Section~\ref{sec:cross_validation_escape}) is positioned as a detection-side complement to these prediction-side cartographies, not as a competitor.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:250:A particularly relevant finding from EVEREST is that the performance gap between methods varies by viral family: alignment-based methods such as EVE consistently outperform PLMs across most viral proteins, but the magnitude of this advantage differs substantially between, for example, influenza HA and SARS-CoV-2 Spike.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:252:AlphaMissense~\cite{cheng2023alphamissense} demonstrated proteome-wide variant classification using an AlphaFold-derived architecture, though its focus on human proteins limits direct viral applicability.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:254:MutBench's unique contribution is the \textit{scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction analysis}: while EVEREST establishes that method performance varies across viruses, MutBench quantifies this interaction through three-way ANOVA ($\omega^2 = 0.296$) and demonstrates that the choice of \textit{biological information source} (not just the computational method) is the dominant performance factor. This finding---that the optimal information source is pathogen-dependent within the 20-type/39-variant design, with the interaction as the largest modeled variance component---has no counterpart in EVEREST or ProteinGym, which treat the scoring/feature set as fixed.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:255:Specifically, MutBench provides three capabilities absent in EVEREST and other VEP benchmarks:
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:256:(1)~quantification of the scoring--pathogen interaction through three-way ANOVA, revealing that the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$; 95\% CI [0.195, 0.333]) is the largest modeled variance component (within-cell residual $\omega^2 \approx 0.39$);
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:257:(2)~cross-validation via vaccine escape enrichment for the 3 of 11 pathogens with curated escape annotations, with HIV-1 (7.19$\times$, Bonferroni-corrected $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$; escape set 82\% disjoint from Layer~A) as the primary external anchor and H3N2 9.36$\times$ reported as a self-consistency check given 69\% Layer~A overlap (circularity audit in Table~\ref{tab:vaccine_escape_stage3});
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:259:Furthermore, MutBench introduces the vaccine escape cross-validation paradigm with a per-pathogen circularity audit: HIV-1 provides the cleanest external validation, while H3N2 and SARS-CoV-2 contribute self-consistency and exploratory evidence respectively---a distinction absent from EVEREST or ProteinGym.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:269:& \textbf{MutBench} & \textbf{ViroGym} & \textbf{EVEREST v3} & \textbf{ProteinGym v1.3} & \textbf{Bailey 2018} \\
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:280:\footnotesize Direct performance comparison between MutBench and ProteinGym/EVEREST is not possible because the tasks differ fundamentally: VEP benchmarks evaluate Spearman correlation between predicted and measured fitness effects (continuous regression), while MutBench evaluates MCC for binary hotspot classification. The benchmarks are complementary rather than competing.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:297:The following chapter presents the MutBench framework in detail, including the construction of multi-layer ground truth datasets for 11 pathogens, the benchmark design comprising 20 scoring types across 6 categories and 14 detection method families, and the factorial ANOVA methodology for quantifying scoring--pathogen interactions.

chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:257:특성별 AUROC는 0.944(Norovirus, homoplasy), 0.805(Influenza~B, homoplasy), 0.787(H3N2, pLDDT), 0.770(Dengue, homoplasy)에 이른다.

chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:268:\textbf{MCC = 0.083의 맥락화.}
chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:269:겸손한 MCC는 분석의 결함이 아니라, 극단적 클래스 불균형(양성 비율 2--5\%) 하에서 위치 수준 이진 분류의 본질적 난이도를 반영한다.
chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:270:유사 분야의 위치 수준 분류도 비슷하게 낮은 절대 메트릭을 산출한다: 암 드라이버 위치 탐지는 MCC $\approx$ 0.1--0.3~\cite{bailey2018comprehensive}, 전사 인자 결합 부위 예측은 F1 $\approx$ 0.3--0.5~\cite{weirauch2013evaluation}를 보고한다.
chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:271:또한 영역 중첩 분석(Section~\ref{sec:oracle_mcc_ceiling})에 따르면, 공간적 근접성($\pm$10 위치)을 고려할 때 평균 oracle MCC가 0.289에서 0.712로 증가하여, 탐지된 핫스팟이 정확히 일치하지 않더라도 ground truth에 공간적으로 근접함을 나타낸다.
chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:272:따라서 위치 정확 MCC는 보수적 하한이며, 영역 수준의 실질적 탐지 정확도는 이보다 현저히 높다.
chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:281:Oracle 상한(MCC = 0.160)은 병원체별 최적 특성 가중치를 사용하더라도 서열 및 구조 파생 특성만으로는 면역 탈출 위치를 완전히 예측할 수 없음을 보여준다.
chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:290:모든 적응적 전략이 EqualWeight보다 열등하였다: kNN 가중 최대 평균 MCC = 0.020, Top-3 AUC 0.049, 상관 인식 0.043으로, EqualWeight의 0.083에 미치지 못한다.
chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:295:그러나 oracle 전략(평균 MCC = 0.160)은 EqualWeight 성능(0.083)을 약 2배로 향상시켜, 레이블 데이터가 있을 때 병원체별 가중치가 진정한 개선을 제공함을 확인한다.
chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:306:\item \textbf{특성 이질성}: 가장 판별력 있는 정보 유형이 병원체마다 다르며(12개 병원체 중 5개 서로 다른 최적 특성), ANOVA에서 관찰된 탐지 family $\times$ pathogen 교호작용($\omega^2 = 0.285$)에 대한 기전적 설명을 제공한다.
chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:307:\item \textbf{간결한 핵심 조합}: 4개 특성 핵심(homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency)이 균일 가중치 하에서 전체 10-feature 앙상블 성능의 98\%를 포착하며, 평균적으로 잡음인 특성(ESM-2, SASA)이 특정 병원체에서는 최적 판별자이다.
chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:308:\item \textbf{실용적 탐색 범위 축소}: 균등 가중 10-feature 통합은 단일 특성 접근법이 유의성에 도달하지 못하는 상황에서 통계적으로 유의한 H3N2 백신 탈출 농축(4.012배, $p = 0.0023$)을 달성하여, 전수 실험 스크리닝을 유도된 조사로 전환한다.
chapters/ch5_adapt.tex:309:\item \textbf{적응적 가중 잠재력}: Oracle 상한(MCC = 0.160 대 EqualWeight 0.083)은 병원체별 특성 가중치가 성능을 2배로 높일 수 있음을 확인하지만, 현재 12개 병원체를 넘어 참조 데이터베이스 확장이 필요하다.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:15:It organizes 10 information types into 20 scoring formulas across 6 categories (frequency, MSA-derived, phylogenetic, structural, AI-based, and composite), defines a three-layer ground truth framework (convergent evolution positives as Layer~A, purifying selection negatives as Layer~B, DMS experimental fitness as Layer~C), introduces the hotspot-score composite metric, and presents a two-stage experimental design combining in-depth SARS-CoV-2 analysis (Stage~1) with large-scale comparison across 11 RNA viruses (Stage~2; see Chapter~\ref{ch:results} for detailed statistics).
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:17:\textbf{Contribution 2. Statistical demonstration that the optimal biological information source differs fundamentally across pathogens ($\omega^2_{\text{scoring} \times \text{pathogen}} = 0.296$), with 9 distinct optimal information types across 11 pathogens and no cross-pathogen generalization (LOPO 0/11).}
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:18:Statistical analysis of the large-scale benchmark results across 11 RNA viruses provided, through two primary analyses (the scoring~$\times$~pathogen ANOVA interaction and the vaccine-escape enrichment) and two null-consistent corroborations (LOPO 0/11 and Friedman) on the same 8{,}580-evaluation dataset, consistent evidence that the optimal biological information source is pathogen-dependent.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:19:First, the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$ at 20-type granularity; 95\% cluster-bootstrap CI [0.195, 0.333]; $\omega^2 = 0.103$ at 6-category granularity as a collinearity-robust lower bound) was the largest identified source of variance among modeled terms in the factorial ANOVA, with within-cell residual ($\omega^2 \approx 0.39$) representing unmodeled variation including the three-way interaction (Chapter~\ref{ch:results} Table~\ref{tab:9pathogen_anova}).
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:20:Second, all 11 pathogens exhibited unique best scoring--detection combinations (11/11 unique best combos), with 9 distinct optimal information types, yielding a mean MCC gap of 0.265 between oracle and generalized performance.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:21:Third, the Friedman test ($p = 0.990$) showed no reliably superior combination across all pathogens, consistent with pathogen-dependent optimality.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:22:Fourth, Leave-One-Pathogen-Out (LOPO) cross-validation yielded a 0/11 agreement result, showing that the optimal information source for one pathogen does not generalize to others.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:24:\textbf{Contribution 3 (two-part).} \textit{(3a) Multi-source integration infrastructure}: a compact 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) captures $\approx$98\% (97.6\%) of the full 10-feature ensemble performance, and EqualWeight integration achieves a statistically significant 4.012-fold H3N2 enrichment ($p = 0.0023$) where single-feature approaches fail. \textit{(3b) Externally-valid vaccine-escape enrichment, anchored on HIV-1}: the Layer-A-disjoint subset of HIV-1 escape positions (37 of 45) yields a direct novel-only enrichment of $7.16\text{--}8.24\times$ (worst-case Bonferroni-adjusted Fisher $p = 5 \times 10^{-12}$); H3N2's 9.36$\times$ is a self-consistency check (69\% Layer~A overlap); SARS-CoV-2 is exploratory after multiple-comparison correction.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:25:A systematic analysis of 10 biological information types (Section~\ref{sec:information_analysis}) reveals that the most informative feature differs across pathogens---homoplasy for Norovirus (AUC\,=\,0.944), pLDDT for H3N2 (0.787), ESM-2 LLR for SARS-CoV-2 (0.586)---and that feature ablation identifies a 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) capturing $\approx$98\% (97.6\%) of integrated performance.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:26:Multi-source integration reduces the experimental search space, achieving H3N2 vaccine escape enrichment of 4.012$\times$ ($p = 0.0023$) where single-information approaches fail to reach significance.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:27:Vaccine-escape enrichment analysis across 3 of 11 pathogens (H3N2, SARS-CoV-2, HIV-1; 2{,}340 evaluations; selected for availability of curated antibody-escape annotations) was audited for circularity against the Layer~A ground truth. \textbf{HIV-1 is the cleanest external validation}: its escape set shares only 8 of 45 positions (18\%) with HIV-1 Layer~A, so the 7.19$\times$ enrichment (Bonferroni-adjusted $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$) primarily reflects detection of positions outside the benchmark's training signal. \textbf{H3N2 should be read as a self-consistency check, not external validation}: 20 of 29 H3N2 escape positions (69\%) are in Layer~A, and on the 9 Layer~A-disjoint (novel) escape positions the top combination's enrichment drops to 7.19$\times$ with Fisher $p = 0.132$ (not significant under any correction), so the headline H3N2 9.36$\times$ predominantly re-measures Layer~A performance under a different label rather than discovering new escape positions. \textbf{SARS-CoV-2 is exploratory only}: the 7.63$\times$ nominal enrichment does not survive Bonferroni correction ($p_{\text{adj}} \to 1$), and 60\% of its escape set overlaps Layer~A. The practical-impact claim of Contribution~3 therefore rests on HIV-1 as the primary external validation, with H3N2 and SARS-CoV-2 contributing self-consistency and exploratory evidence respectively.

chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:114:The oracle ceiling analysis (Section~\ref{subsec:adaptive_weighting_limits}) demonstrated that per-pathogen feature weighting can double performance (MCC = 0.160 vs.\ EqualWeight 0.083), but with only 11 reference pathogens the knowledge base is insufficient for reliable adaptive selection.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:122:Phylogenetic correction would primarily affect pathogens with strong founder effects (e.g., SARS-CoV-2 D614G, which ranks 2nd by H-score but 1,134th by homoplasy), potentially changing the best-performing scoring--detection combinations for those pathogens and improving the overall oracle MCC.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:139:The central result---that the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$; 95\% CI [0.195, 0.333]) is the largest identified modeled variance component, alongside a within-cell residual $\omega^2 \approx 0.39$ that reflects further pathogen-level heterogeneity---empirically supports the algorithm selection principle~\cite{kerschke2019algorithm} and provides evidence that the optimal biological information source is pathogen-dependent.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:140:Nine distinct optimal information types were identified across 11 pathogens, from FUBAR phylogenetic selection scores for H3N2 to protein language models for SARS-CoV-2, indicating that no single information source suffices across the viral landscape.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:141:The concordance between Layer~A benchmark rankings and vaccine escape enrichment is strongest for HIV-1 (7.19$\times$, 82\% of the escape set disjoint from Layer~A; Bonferroni-adjusted $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$), which provides the cleanest external validation; H3N2's headline 9.36$\times$ is largely a self-consistency check given 69\% Layer~A overlap, and SARS-CoV-2's 7.63$\times$ is exploratory (Bonferroni-adjusted $p \to 1$). The benchmark's practical utility for identifying immune evasion positions is therefore established with high confidence only on the Layer~A-disjoint subset exemplified by HIV-1.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:142:Multi-source integration further reduces the experimental search space, with a compact 4-feature core capturing $\approx$98\% (97.6\%) of full-ensemble performance.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:143:These conclusions are bounded by limitations enumerated in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}: the eleven-pathogen scope precludes mixed-effects modeling, a covariate-adjusted (length, positive-rate) variance decomposition has not yet been performed, the LOPO 0/11 result is null-consistent under random-combination permutation, the Layer~A construction is partly literature-curated, the multi-source enrichment claim is statistically anchored by HIV-1, and head-to-head comparison with concurrent benchmarks (ViroGym~\cite{virogym2026}, EVEREST~v3~\cite{gurev2026everest_v3}) remains future work.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:150:The source code of the MutBench framework, benchmark scripts, ground truth definitions for 11 pathogens, and configuration files necessary for reproducing all experiments will be made available at the GitHub repository (\url{https://github.com/hwijun/mutbench}).
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:152:The benchmark can be reproduced with three commands: (1)~feature computation (\texttt{python compute\_features.py --pathogen H3N2}), (2)~detection evaluation (\texttt{python run\_stage3\_full\_detectors.py}), and (3)~statistical analysis (\texttt{python analyze\_stage3\_stats.py}). The full 8{,}580-evaluation benchmark (20 scoring types $\times$ 39 detectors $\times$ 11 pathogens) completes in 25 seconds on a single workstation (measured: 24.96s on an Intel i7 with RTX 4090, without GPU dependency for the benchmark itself). Feature computation for a new pathogen requires approximately 15--20 minutes including MSA construction, frequency/entropy calculation, homoplasy inference, and ESM-2 scoring; structural features (pLDDT, SASA) are optional and require an AlphaFold or experimental structure when available.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:157:All stochastic processes (bootstrap resampling, subsampling) used a fixed random seed (42) for reproducibility.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:158:Pathogen sequence data were collected from NCBI GenBank, and SARS-CoV-2 DMS data were obtained from the original data provided by Dadonaite et al.~\cite{dadonaite2023dms, dadonaite2024nature}.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:13:\label{sec:bootstrap_interpretation}
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:15:The wide 95\% confidence intervals observed in region-level BCa bootstrap (e.g., MutClust-Hybrid [0.323, 0.635]) reflect region-dependent recall sensitivity in small samples ($n = 7$): resamples dominated by high-signal regions (RBD) inflate recall, while low-signal-only resamples deflate it.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:16:Nevertheless, pairwise bootstrap comparisons show that differences between methods are significant ($p < 0.001$), because paired evaluation on the same resample cancels region-combination variability.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:33:A more subtle concern is that Layer~A positions (convergent evolution) could correlate with mutation frequency at the \emph{per-position} level, which can make frequency-based scoring appear structurally strong. A per-pathogen audit of the point-biserial correlation between Layer~A membership and per-position frequency finds a mean $|\rho| = 0.12$ across the 11 pathogens (range $[-0.06, +0.33]$): HCV (+0.33), Influenza~B (+0.26) and Norovirus (+0.23) show moderate positive correlations, while SARS-CoV-2 ($\rho \approx 0$), MERS ($\approx 0$) and EV-A71 ($\approx 0$) are essentially uncorrelated. The effect is therefore pathogen-specific rather than uniform, and is driven by ground-truth curation style: pathogens whose Layer~A uses hypervariable/epochal-variant criteria (HCV, Influenza~B, Norovirus) couple more strongly with frequency than pathogens whose Layer~A uses phylogenetically-confirmed convergent positions (SARS-CoV-2, H3N2).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:35:To provide a frequency-independent validation dimension, Layer~C (DMS experimental fitness) is used where available (6 of 11 pathogens), and the vaccine escape enrichment analysis (Section~\ref{sec:vaccine_escape}) provides partial external cross-validation: HIV-1 (82\% of its escape set disjoint from Layer~A) is the cleanest external anchor, whereas H3N2's 69\% Layer~A/escape overlap means that the H3N2 enrichment re-measures benchmark performance more than it provides independent replication. The circularity audit in Chapter~\ref{ch:results} Table~\ref{tab:vaccine_escape_stage3} reports novel-only enrichment values that quantify this distinction.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:47:The H-score saturation phenomenon observed in temporal validation (Section~\ref{sec:temporal}) reveals a fundamental limitation of reference-based metrics: in 2024--2025 data, all 1,259 Spike positions (post-truncation alignment) have non-zero H-scores with a standard deviation of only 0.098, resulting in loss of discriminatory power.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:59:The ground-truth-dependent method rankings observed within SARS-CoV-2 foreshadow the pathogen-dependent rankings revealed in the cross-pathogen benchmark.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:68:Cross-pathogen validation revealed pathogen-dependent performance: HIV-1 showed significant discrimination (AUC = 0.706, $p = 0.0002$), H3N2 showed a weak trend (AUC = 0.561, $p = 0.147$), and HCV failed entirely (AUC = 0.390) due to parsimony saturation in its hypervariable regions.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:70:This mirrors the detection-level finding of the main benchmark: the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$) demonstrates that the optimal scoring strategy depends on pathogen-specific characteristics.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:80:The underlying cause is that pathogen-specific genomic characteristics create fundamentally different signal landscapes---for example, H3N2's uniformly nonzero H-scores neutralize threshold-based seed detection, while MERS's sparse genome favors weak-signal detectors.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:82:A notable finding is the asymmetry between scoring and detection contributions: the detection method family main effect ($\omega^2 = 0.013$) is the smallest variance component, approximately 23 times smaller than the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$). This implies that \textit{the choice of input information} matters far more than \textit{the choice of detection algorithm}. Practically, this means that effort should be directed toward selecting the right information source for each pathogen rather than optimizing detection algorithm parameters.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:85:The ESM-2 cross-paradigm validation (Section~\ref{subsec:esm_validation}) reinforces this: ESM-LLR is the top-ranked feature for SARS-CoV-2 but substantially outperformed by homoplasy for Norovirus (AUC $= 0.763$ vs.\ $0.944$), confirming that no single scoring paradigm dominates.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:92:\textbf{EVEREST}~\cite{gurev2025everest} benchmarked variant effect prediction (VEP) methods across 45 viral DMS datasets and found that protein language models substantially underperform alignment-based approaches on viral proteins, with prediction reliability varying dramatically across pathogens. This parallels MutBench's finding that the optimal \textit{information source} is pathogen-dependent, with the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction as the largest variance component. However, EVEREST evaluates per-mutation fitness prediction (continuous Spearman correlation), whereas MutBench evaluates per-region hotspot detection (binary MCC classification). The convergence of both studies on the pathogen-dependence conclusion---despite addressing fundamentally different problems---strengthens the generality of this finding.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:94:\textbf{Maher et al.}~\cite{maher2022predicting} analyzed multiple feature types (frequency, phylogenetic, structural) for predicting SARS-CoV-2 variant emergence and found that combining features outperformed any single feature. MutBench's EqualWeight integration result (H3N2 escape enrichment 4.012$\times$, $p = 0.0023$, where single features did not reach significance) is consistent with this finding and extends it to 11 pathogens, showing that the benefit of multi-source integration generalizes beyond SARS-CoV-2.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:96:\textbf{Hie et al.}~\cite{hie2021learning} demonstrated that protein language model semantic similarity captures viral escape potential. MutBench confirms this for specific pathogens: semantic change is the best-performing scoring type for EV-A71 (MCC = 0.260), but not for others (e.g., HCV, where frequency dominates). This pathogen-specificity was not observable in Hie et al.'s single-pathogen analysis.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:100:\textbf{ProteinGym}~\cite{notin2023proteingym} showed that VEP model performance varies across the 217 DMS assays in its benchmark. While ProteinGym focuses on human and model organism proteins, MutBench demonstrates the same pattern in viral proteins, with the additional finding that the choice of \textit{input information type}---not just the computational model---is the dominant performance factor.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:102:In summary, the pathogen-dependence of optimal methods is not unique to MutBench but appears to be a general principle across variant effect prediction (EVEREST, ProteinGym), feature analysis (Maher et al.), escape prediction (Hie et al.), and driver detection (Bailey et al.). MutBench's contribution is to quantify this dependence through variance decomposition ($\omega^2 = 0.296$ at 20-type granularity; 0.103 at 6-category granularity as a collinearity-robust lower bound) and to illustrate practical consequence through vaccine-escape cross-validation, with HIV-1 (7.19-fold enrichment, 82\% disjoint from Layer~A) as the primary external anchor and H3N2 (9.36-fold) as a self-consistency check given 69\% Layer~A/escape overlap.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:108:\label{sec:oracle_mcc_ceiling}
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:110:The mean oracle MCC across 11 pathogens is 0.341 (range: 0.196--0.660; Table~\ref{tab:9pathogen_best}), which appears low but is explained by three structural factors: position-level exact matching (off-by-one counts as false positive), extreme class imbalance (positive rates 0.7\%--15.9\%), and ground truth stringency (only literature-confirmed sites).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:111:The oracle is unambiguously non-random (113 standard deviations above the random baseline mean of 0.001), and comparable to position-level metrics in other domains (e.g., TFBS prediction F1 = 0.3--0.5~\cite{weirauch2013evaluation}).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:113:Region-overlap analysis (Table~\ref{tab:region_overlap_mcc}) quantifies the effect of evaluation stringency: under $\pm5$ position windows, mean oracle MCC increases from 0.341 to 0.472 (38\% improvement), with Influenza~B reaching 0.894. Notably, some pathogens (HCV, Norovirus) show \textit{decreased} MCC under window expansion because their oracle detections are already precise---window expansion dilutes precision by including non-functional neighboring positions.

chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:151:The mean oracle recall across 11 pathogens is 0.552 (Table~\ref{tab:precision_at_k}), indicating that the best combination for each pathogen detects approximately half of the known convergent evolution positions. While this may appear insufficient for safety-critical applications, three observations provide context.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:153:First, \textit{the missed positions are not randomly distributed}. Positions with low recall tend to be those where the convergent evolution signal is weakest---positions documented in only 3 lineages (the minimum threshold for Layer~A inclusion), or positions where the selective advantage is epistatic (dependent on other mutations) rather than individually strong. For SARS-CoV-2, the 8 undetected Layer~A positions (recall = 0.680, 17/25 detected) are predominantly NTD supersite positions where immune evasion operates through conformational changes rather than direct frequency elevation.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:155:Second, \textit{multi-source integration recovers positions missed by single-information approaches}. For H3N2, frequency-based scoring misses antigenic site~B positions (155, 159, 160) that are structurally constrained, but the EqualWeight ensemble captures them through the pLDDT and homoplasy components (Section~\ref{subsec:search_space_reduction}). This complementarity---where different information types detect different subsets of positions---is the mechanistic basis for the dominant scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:157:Third, \textit{region-level coverage is substantially higher than position-level recall}. Under $\pm$10 position windows (approximately one epitope width), the mean MCC increases from 0.341 to 0.454, and Influenza~B reaches 0.924. Positions scored as ``missed'' in exact evaluation are often detected within 1--2 residues of the true position---close enough to guide experimental prioritization, which is the practical goal.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:164:Returning to the three problems identified in Chapter~\ref{ch:introduction}: the standardised evaluation framework is provided by the three-layer ground truth and hotspot-score metric (Contribution~1); pathogen-dependence is quantified by the interaction effect ($\omega^2 = 0.296$) and corroborated by LOPO 0/11 (Contribution~2); cross-validation against vaccine-escape positions establishes practical relevance, anchored by HIV-1 (Contribution~3).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:170:Vaccine escape validation (Table~\ref{tab:vaccine_escape_stage3}) showed enrichment values of 9.36$\times$ for H3N2, 7.19$\times$ for HIV-1, and 7.63$\times$ for SARS-CoV-2 (nominal Fisher's exact $p$-values). Under Bonferroni correction across 780 combinations, HIV-1 ($p_{\text{adj}} = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$) and H3N2 ($p_{\text{adj}} = 2.6 \times 10^{-5}$) survive while SARS-CoV-2 does not. The circularity audit in Chapter~\ref{ch:results} further distinguishes HIV-1 (82\% of escape set disjoint from Layer~A; external validation) from H3N2 (69\% Layer~A overlap; self-consistency check).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:171:The multi-feature EqualWeight integration further achieves statistically significant H3N2 escape enrichment (4.012$\times$, $p = 0.0023$) where single-feature approaches do not. The primary practical value lies in \textit{reducing the experimental search space} rather than achieving high absolute prediction accuracy (see Section~\ref{subsec:search_space_reduction} for detailed discussion).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:173:While LOPO cross-validation yields 0/11 generalization, MutBench provides practical value through three mechanisms: (1)~the family-level scoring recommendation table (Table~\ref{tab:scoring_recommendation} in this chapter) provides coarse-grained guidance based on virus family characteristics; (2)~the 4-feature EqualWeight ensemble achieves 4.012-fold vaccine escape enrichment without requiring pathogen-specific optimization; and (3)~for any new pathogen with $\geq$200 sequences, the full 8,580-evaluation benchmark completes in approximately 25~seconds on a single workstation, making exhaustive evaluation operationally feasible.

chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:199:\paragraph{Three-tier evidence rule.} Pathogens are assigned to one of three evidence tiers using two operational criteria evaluated jointly: (i)~\emph{Bonferroni survival} of the Fisher's exact $p$-value across 780 scoring--detection combinations ($p_{\text{adj}} < 0.05$), and (ii)~\emph{Layer~A independence}, defined as fewer than one-third of escape positions overlapping the pathogen's Layer~A set ($|\text{escape} \cap \text{Layer A}| / |\text{escape}| < 33\%$). A pathogen passing both criteria is classified as a \textbf{primary external anchor} (HIV-1: 18\% overlap, $p_{\text{adj}} = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$); a pathogen passing only (i)~is a \textbf{self-consistency check} (H3N2: 69\% overlap, $p_{\text{adj}} = 2.6 \times 10^{-5}$); a pathogen passing neither is reported as \textbf{exploratory} (SARS-CoV-2: $p_{\text{adj}} > 0.05$). The 33\% overlap threshold separates the three observed pathogens into distinct tiers without intermediate values; sensitivity to the threshold (25\%, 33\%, 50\%) does not change tier assignments for these three cases. With only three pathogens any threshold in $(18\%, 60\%)$ produces the same partition; the rule is therefore calibrated on observed data and explicitly underpowered as a *predictive* rule for new pathogens. Future cycles with additional escape-annotated pathogens will test whether the 33\% threshold remains the correct cut-point; the present work uses it as a transparent decision rule, not a generalised threshold.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:201:HIV-1 is the cleanest external validation: its escape set shares only 8 of 45 positions (18\%) with HIV-1 Layer~A, so the 7.19$\times$ enrichment (Bonferroni-adjusted $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$) primarily reflects detection of positions outside the benchmark's training signal. A direct novel-only re-test on the 37 Layer~A-disjoint positions (best combination freq~$+$~Wavelet~$t = 1.5$) yields enrichment in the range $7.16\text{--}8.24\times$ depending on how many of the 8 escape~$\cap$~Layer-A positions the detector also captures (sensitivity $k \in \{0, \ldots, 8\}$); even the conservative worst case ($k = 8$, all overlap positions detected) gives $7.16\times$ with Fisher $p = 5.0 \times 10^{-12}$, which survives Bonferroni correction ($\times 780$) by more than nine orders of magnitude.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:202:In contrast, H3N2's 9.36$\times$ is largely a self-consistency check: 20 of 29 escape positions (69\%) already lie in H3N2 Layer~A, so the high enrichment predominantly re-measures Layer~A performance. Restricting the calculation to the 9 Layer~A-disjoint (novel) escape positions drops the enrichment to 7.19$\times$ with Fisher $p = 0.132$ (not significant; Chapter~\ref{ch:results} Table~\ref{tab:vaccine_escape_stage3} circularity audit).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:203:SARS-CoV-2's 7.63$\times$ nominal enrichment does not survive Bonferroni correction and is reported as exploratory only.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:205:The benchmark is \emph{not a circular artifact} in the algorithmic sense (ground truth and scoring are computed independently), but the practical-value claim of Contribution~3 is carried primarily by HIV-1, with H3N2 and SARS-CoV-2 contributing self-consistency and exploratory evidence.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:207:\textbf{Concurrent-benchmark task-orthogonality.} The MutBench panel overlaps with ViroGym (HIV, SARS-CoV-2, H3N2 are common) and EVEREST~v3 (HIV, SARS-CoV-2 forecasting clades), so a head-to-head leaderboard appears feasible in principle. We do not run one in this dissertation because the metric universes are structurally non-overlapping: ViroGym and EVEREST optimise per-variant fitness Spearman against DMS, while MutBench optimises per-region binary MCC against the 3-layer ground truth; converting between the two requires either (a) thresholding fitness predictions at a top-$k$ cutoff to obtain a binary region call (which throws away the continuous information ViroGym/EVEREST were optimised for), or (b) summarising MutBench detections into a fitness ranking (which throws away the spatial-clustering information MutBench was optimised for). Either reduction biases the comparison toward the receiving format. The principled task-aligned subset evaluation (binarise fitness predictions at top-$k$ thresholds matched to MutBench's positive-rate per pathogen, then compare MCC on the shared HIV/SARS-CoV-2/H3N2 panel) is queued as a defense-week sprint item (Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion} Table~\ref{tab:limitations_summary}); the present cycle's contribution is the *structural orthogonality argument* itself, which removes the head-to-head as a knock-down objection.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:210:The EVEREST study and its v3 expansion~\cite{gurev2025everest,gurev2026everest_v3} demonstrate that even with 45 DMS datasets, current models fail to reliably predict mutations in over half of the 40 WHO priority RNA viruses, with reliability worst for surface glycoproteins---an external finding that independently corroborates the LOPO 0/11 non-transferability reported in Chapter~\ref{ch:results}. For H3N2 specifically, the antigenic-cartography lineage of Smith et al.~\cite{smith2004antigenic} and the recent PLM-based extensions of PLANT~\cite{plant2025antigenic} and Shah et al.~\cite{shah2024h3n2ml} target a prediction task complementary to MutBench's region-level detection; the 69\% Layer~A overlap reported above should therefore be interpreted as task-internal self-consistency rather than as a head-to-head antigenic-prediction claim.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:217:Given SARS-CoV-2's generation time ({$\sim$}5 days) and sequence submission delay ({$\sim$}14 days), a minimum 4-week window is required for real-time TC-freq alerts. A fundamental methodological limitation affecting all frequency-based approaches is phylogenetic non-independence.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:219:For public health practitioners, MutBench results can be operationalized through the following workflow when a novel pathogen or variant emerges: (1)~compute the 20 scoring types from the available MSA (requiring only sequence data and publicly available tools: MAFFT for alignment, HyPhy for FUBAR, ESM-2 for PLM scores, AlphaFold2 for structural features); (2)~if the pathogen belongs to a family already represented in MutBench (e.g., Coronaviridae, Orthomyxoviridae, Flaviviridae), use the family-level scoring recommendation from Table~\ref{tab:scoring_recommendation} as a starting point; (3)~if the pathogen is novel, apply the EqualWeight ensemble as a conservative baseline, which achieves 98\% of full-feature performance with only 4 core features (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency). This workflow integrates with existing surveillance platforms such as Nextstrain~\cite{nextstrain2018hadfield} and GISAID~\cite{shu2017gisaid}, which already provide the MSA inputs required by MutBench.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:231:Compute scoring features in order of increasing computational cost: (i)~frequency and Shannon entropy from the MSA (seconds); (ii)~homoplasy counts via Fitch parsimony on an inferred phylogenetic tree (2--5 minutes); (iii)~ESM-2 log-likelihood ratios, requiring a GPU (3--5 minutes per protein); (iv)~structural features such as surface accessibility and interface proximity, requiring an AlphaFold2~\cite{jumper2021alphafold} predicted structure or an experimental PDB entry when available. Steps (i)--(iii) are applicable to any pathogen with $\geq$200 sequences and require no specialized hardware beyond a single GPU for ESM-2 inference; step (iv) can be omitted when no structural model exists, with moderate impact on detection performance. When structural features are available, the 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) captures 98\% of full-ensemble performance; without pLDDT, the remaining 3 features (homoplasy, entropy, frequency) still provide the dominant scoring signals.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:234:Table~\ref{tab:scoring_recommendation} provides empirically grounded recommendations based on which scoring category achieved the highest mean MCC for each virus family in the benchmark. Users should select the recommended category as a starting point and, if computational resources permit, evaluate additional categories.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:256:Apply KDE or Wavelet-based detection as robust defaults (Section~\ref{sec:external_comparison}). If ground truth positions are available (e.g., from DMS experiments or literature), compute the hotspot-score metric. When scoring features are pre-computed, detection and evaluation across all 39 detector configurations completes in under 3~seconds per pathogen (the full 8,580-evaluation benchmark requires approximately 25~seconds).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:260:For resource-constrained settings, the 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) achieves statistically indistinguishable performance from the full 10-feature ensemble (MCC 0.081 vs.\ 0.083) while requiring only MSA-based computation and a single AlphaFold2 query---eliminating the need for GPU-intensive ESM-2 inference and reducing runtime to under 10 minutes per pathogen.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:266:All detection methods in this study implicitly assume independence between sequences; however, SARS-CoV-2 sequences are phylogenetically structured, and frequency-based approaches cannot distinguish positive selection from founder effects (e.g., D614G;~\cite{korber2020tracking}).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:282:\textbf{Temporal window dependence}: An additional unstandardized factor is the analysis time window. The 11 pathogens in this benchmark were analyzed using sequences spanning different time ranges: SARS-CoV-2 covers approximately 2 years of pandemic evolution (2020--2021), while H3N2 encompasses decades of seasonal circulation.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:283:Temporal analysis on SARS-CoV-2 Spike across three 6-month windows reveals that feature discriminative power changes substantially: frequency AUC increases from 0.337 (2020-H1) to 0.472 (2021-H1), and entropy AUC from 0.328 to 0.507, as mean Shannon entropy rises 10-fold (0.126 to 1.241) with accumulating diversity.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:289:ESM-2~\cite{lin2023esm2} was trained on UniRef50/UniRef90, which contains viral protein sequences, and the 11 target proteins in our benchmark (e.g., SARS-CoV-2 Spike, HIV-1 gp120, H3N2 HA) are likely present in the training corpus.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:291:However, this concern applies uniformly to all 11 pathogens in the analysis, so while absolute performance levels may be biased upward, the relative cross-pathogen comparisons---which constitute our main finding---remain valid.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:293:Future work should evaluate protein language models trained on databases that exclude viral sequences to quantify the magnitude of this potential bias. \textbf{Concurrent-benchmark reconciliation}: EVEREST v3 reports that PLMs underperform alignment-based methods on viral DMS \emph{fitness regression}, while the present work finds PLMs winning on 2 of 11 pathogens for region-level \emph{detection} (RSV best ESM-2 LLR; SARS-CoV-2 best Tranception). The two findings are compatible because the tasks differ structurally (per-variant continuous Spearman vs.\ per-region binary MCC), and the fact that Norovirus's best is homoplasy (AUC 0.944) rather than a PLM is exactly the pattern leakage-driven inflation would not predict.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:297:Among the 20 scoring types, several share an underlying information source (e.g., freq, freq\_with\_indel, and rare\_freq are all frequency-derived). This partial collinearity could inflate the apparent number of independent scoring levels in the ANOVA. When scoring types are aggregated to the 6-category level, the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction shrinks substantially: a supplementary two-way ANOVA with 6 scoring categories yields $\omega^2_{\text{category} \times \text{pathogen}} = 0.103$, which is below Cohen's large-effect threshold ($\omega^2 \geq 0.14$) but above the medium threshold ($\omega^2 \geq 0.06$), and is comparable in magnitude to the pathogen main effect ($\omega^2 = 0.117$). The interaction therefore remains practically non-trivial even after collinearity correction, but the ``largest source of variance'' framing in the 20-type model is partly driven by fine-grained distinctions within categories; readers should interpret the 6-category $\omega^2 = 0.103$ as the collinearity-robust lower bound and the 20-type $\omega^2 = 0.296$ as the upper bound on the pathogen-scoring interaction depending on how ``scoring type'' is defined.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:299:A methodological limitation concerns the \emph{winner's curse}~\cite{ioannidis2008winner}: with 780 candidate combinations searched per pathogen and the highest-MCC combination retained, the reported top-1 enrichment is an upper-envelope estimate rather than a typical value (the Bonferroni-survivor mean enrichment is materially lower; H3N2 mean $\approx 4.7\times$ vs.\ top $9.36\times$). The winner's-curse formulation is one face of the broader question of multiple testing correction when selecting the best scoring--detection combination per pathogen. At the detection-family level (20 scoring $\times$ 14 families = 280 combinations evaluated per pathogen), the probability that 11 out of 11 pathogens exhibit unique best combinations by chance alone is approximately 82\% under uniform random assignment ($\prod_{i=0}^{10} (280-i)/280 \approx 0.820$); at the parameter-variant level (20 scoring $\times$ 39 variants = 780 combinations, as reported in Section~\ref{subsec:9pathogen_statistical}), the same probability is approximately 93\%. The choice of aggregation level matters: the family-level calculation is the more conservative reference for cross-pathogen uniqueness because parameter-variant collapsing to families reduces the effective combinatorial space. However, several factors mitigate this concern: (1)~the best combinations are not merely unique but involve 9~distinct scoring \textit{types} from 4~of~6 categories, which has much lower random probability; (2)~the ANOVA interaction effect ($\omega^2 = 0.296$) quantifies systematic rather than chance variation; and (3)~the vaccine escape enrichment cross-validation confirms that benchmark-optimal methods also achieve the highest enrichment on independently curated escape positions. Nevertheless, future work should apply permutation-based significance testing to determine whether each pathogen's best combination is statistically distinguishable from alternatives.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:301:The three-way ANOVA treats pathogen as a fixed effect, which is appropriate for inference about these 11~specific pathogens but does not support generalization to all RNA viruses. A mixed-effects model treating pathogen as a random effect would enable broader inference; however, with only 11~pathogen-level observations, frequentist random-effect estimation is unreliable (Bolker et al.~\cite{bolker2009glmm} recommend $\geq$5--6 levels per random factor, ideally more). A natural alternative for the small-$n$ regime is \emph{Bayesian hierarchical (partial-pooling) modeling}, which we have additionally fit. With half-Cauchy priors on the between-scoring, between-pathogen, between-family, interaction-, and residual-scale parameters and a vague Normal prior on the grand mean, the NUTS posterior over the cell-level model (PyMC 5.28; 2~chains $\times$ 800 draws after 800 tuning steps; $\hat R \leq 1.01$ for all variance components) yields a posterior mean of $\omega^2_{\text{scoring} \times \text{pathogen}} = 0.252$ with 95\% HDI $[0.188, 0.314]$ and posterior probability $\Pr(\omega^2_{\text{int}} > 0.14) = 0.996$. The partial-pooling estimate sits slightly below the fixed-effect point (0.296) as expected from variance shrinkage, but the credible-interval lower bound (0.188) still essentially coincides with the cluster-bootstrap lower bound (0.195) and remains above Cohen's large-effect threshold ($\omega^2 > 0.14$) under both inferential frames. As the benchmark expands to 20--30+ pathogens, frequentist mixed-effects modeling additionally becomes feasible by the Bolker criterion.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:306:Per-pathogen oracle MCC correlates strongly with two technical covariates that are not modeled in the three-way ANOVA: protein length (Spearman $\rho = -0.73$, $p = 0.011$ across the 11 pathogens) and Layer~A positive rate (Spearman $\rho = +0.64$, $p = 0.035$). That is, shorter proteins with a higher Layer~A positive rate (e.g., H3N2 HA, Norovirus capsid) systematically attain higher oracle MCC than longer proteins with sparse Layer~A (e.g., HCV E1E2). Because MCC itself is bounded by class balance, a portion of the reported $\omega^2_{\text{scoring} \times \text{pathogen}} = 0.296$ may reflect this structural heterogeneity rather than intrinsic biological signal. A formal ANCOVA fit (statsmodels Type~II OLS on the cell-level grid with $\log(\text{length})$ and Layer~A positive rate as continuous covariates) confirms the directional prediction: the pathogen main effect collapses from $\omega^2 = 0.108$ to essentially zero (covariates absorb it entirely, as expected since both are pathogen-constant), and the scoring~$\times$~pathogen interaction \emph{rises} from $\omega^2 = 0.234$ at the cell-level baseline to $\omega^2 = 0.264$ after adjustment ($p < 10^{-167}$ in both fits). Family~$\times$~pathogen also rises modestly (0.081 $\to$ 0.091), and scoring/family main effects are unchanged. The fixed-effect headline of 0.296 reported at the evaluation level (8{,}580 observations) is mechanically slightly higher than the cell-level 0.234 because aggregating to family-level mean MCC reduces within-cell residual; the \emph{relative shift} from baseline to ANCOVA-adjusted ($+0.030$) is the load-bearing quantity, and it confirms that the interaction is amplified rather than attenuated by technical-covariate adjustment.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:308:\textbf{Layer-A curation-protocol subset analysis.} A second concern raised by the curation heterogeneity (Section~\ref{sec:gt_heterogeneity}) is that the interaction might be inflated by the most idiosyncratic Layer~A definitions (HCV's HVR diversifying selection and Norovirus's epochal-variant positions). Re-fitting the cell-level ANOVA on the HCV-excluded subset ($n = 10$) yields $\omega^2_{\text{scoring} \times \text{pathogen}} = 0.199$; further excluding Norovirus ($n = 9$) yields $\omega^2 = 0.187$. Both restricted estimates remain firmly in Cohen's medium-to-large range, demonstrating that the pathogen-adaptive finding is not driven by the two pathogens with non-convergent-evolution Layer~A construction. Restricting further to the four phylogenetically-derived Layer~A pathogens (SARS-CoV-2, H3N2, MERS, EV-A71; $n = 4$) gives $\omega^2 = 0.137$, still above Cohen's medium threshold despite the loss of statistical power. The pathogen-adaptive conclusion should therefore be read as holding \emph{within the 20-type/39-variant design and the 11-pathogen sample}, and independent validation on additional pathogens with matched length/positive-rate is a priority for follow-up work.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:311:The 20 scoring types do not operate under identical conditions. Frequency and entropy scores require only the MSA, making them the most standardized. Phylogenetic scores (FUBAR, dN/dS, homoplasy) additionally depend on phylogenetic tree quality, which varies across pathogens: H3N2's well-sampled multi-decade tree provides more reliable dN/dS estimates than MERS's sparse 5-year phylogeny. Structure-based scores (pLDDT, SASA) depend on predicted structure accuracy, which is higher for well-characterized proteins (SARS-CoV-2 Spike) than for less-studied ones (EV-A71 VP1). AI-based scores inherit biases from their training data, as discussed above.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:320:For SARS-CoV-2 and H3N2, Layer~A positions are phylogenetically confirmed convergent evolution sites---positions where identical mutations arose independently in multiple lineages.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:326:The heterogeneous Layer~A definitions across pathogens (convergent evolution for SARS-CoV-2/H3N2, epochal variants for Norovirus, hypervariable regions for HCV) mean that MCC values are not directly comparable across pathogens in absolute terms. The ANOVA interaction effect should therefore be interpreted as reflecting systematic variation in \textit{relative} method rankings across pathogens, rather than absolute performance differences. The consistency of this finding under category-level aggregation ($\omega^2_{\text{category} \times \text{pathogen}} = 0.103$) provides additional robustness.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:333:The 11 pathogens were selected to systematically cover 8 major RNA virus families (Coronaviridae, Orthomyxoviridae, Retroviridae, Pneumoviridae, Flaviviridae, Caliciviridae, Rhabdoviridae, Picornaviridae), representing the primary taxonomic diversity of RNA viruses with pandemic potential.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:335:Despite the small sample size ($n=11$), the Friedman test yielded $p=0.990$, indicating that no single method can be reliably distinguished as superior across all pathogens. This is consistent with the LOPO finding (0/11 match rate) that each pathogen requires a unique best-performing combination. \textbf{Sampling-quality vs.\ pathogen-dependence}: the smallest-sample pathogens (Rabies $n_{\text{seq}} = 2{,}038$ but truncated 491 AA; EV-A71 $n_{\text{seq}} = 662$, 261 AA) do attain the lowest oracle MCCs (0.248, 0.260), so a sampling-quality confound is not zero. However, the technical-covariate sensitivity analysis (Section~\ref{sec:scoring_input_heterogeneity}, $\rho_L = -0.73$, $\rho_P = +0.64$) shows the joint covariate effect is subsumed by the pathogen main effect ($\omega^2 = 0.117$), and the scoring~$\times$~pathogen interaction (0.296) is a within-pathogen quantity that survives this absorption (see the ANCOVA bound there). Excluding the two smallest-sample pathogens (re-running the ANOVA on $n = 9$) shifts the headline interaction by less than the cluster-bootstrap CI half-width, so the pathogen-dependence finding is not a small-sample artifact of the two weakest panels.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:337:The LOPO result should be interpreted with caution given the small sample size ($n = 11$). With only 10 training pathogens per fold, the power to detect a generalizable best combination is inherently limited. The 0/11 match rate is consistent with two interpretations: (1)~truly pathogen-specific optimality with no cross-pathogen generalization, or (2)~insufficient sample size to identify a robust generalizable pattern. The large mean performance gap (0.265 MCC) between oracle and generalized predictions supports interpretation~(1), but a definitive distinction requires a larger pathogen panel.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:339:A methodological caveat is that the 11 pathogens are not phylogenetically independent: three pairs share viral families (SARS-CoV-2 and MERS in Coronaviridae, H3N2 and Influenza~B in Orthomyxoviridae, HCV and Dengue in Flaviviridae). The ANOVA treats pathogens as independent blocks, which may underestimate standard errors for pathogen-related effects. However, within each family pair, the best-performing scoring types differ (FUBAR Bayes factor for H3N2 vs.\ frequency for Influenza~B; frequency for HCV vs.\ entropy\_with\_indel for Dengue; Tranception for SARS-CoV-2 vs.\ frequency for MERS), indicating that phylogenetic relatedness does not determine method preference. This within-family heterogeneity strengthens rather than weakens the pathogen-adaptive finding.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:344:The AI-based scoring types (ESM-2 LLR, Tranception, semantic change, stability predictors) were evaluated using pre-trained models without virus-specific fine-tuning. The performance of these models is constrained by the composition of their training data: ESM-2 was trained on UniRef50 (general proteins), which includes limited representation of rapidly evolving viral surface proteins. Fine-tuning on viral protein families or using virus-specific language models could potentially improve performance but was not evaluated in this study. Recent work on CoVFit~\cite{covfit2025}, which fine-tunes ESM-2 on SARS-CoV-2 epidemiological and DMS data, demonstrates that pathogen-specific adaptation of PLMs can substantially improve fitness prediction---consistent with MutBench's central finding that the optimal information source is pathogen-dependent. Additionally, the comparison between sequence-based (ESM-2) and structure-conditioned (stability\_structural) predictors does not control for the quality of input structures, which varies across pathogens depending on the availability of experimentally determined structures versus AlphaFold2 predictions.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:345:This may introduce systematic bias: pathogens with high-quality experimental structures (e.g., SARS-CoV-2 Spike) may show inflated structural feature importance relative to pathogens relying on AlphaFold2 predictions. Controlling for structure source (experimental vs.\ predicted) in future analyses would strengthen the structural feature comparisons.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:347:The MSA sequences used in this benchmark were downloaded from NCBI GenBank without controlling for geographic or temporal sampling bias. Surveillance intensity varies dramatically across pathogens and regions: SARS-CoV-2 sequences are dominated by high-income country submissions during 2020--2022, while Rabies and EV-A71 sequences reflect more geographically diverse but temporally sparse sampling. This sampling heterogeneity may inflate mutation frequencies at founder-effect positions in over-sampled lineages (e.g., SARS-CoV-2 D614G) while underrepresenting diversity in under-sampled regions. The Layer~A ground truth partially mitigates this concern by requiring independent emergence across multiple lineages, but Layer~A position counts themselves may be biased toward well-studied pathogens.

review/2026-04-17/phase4_professor.md:29:## Q2. 8,580 evaluations에서 data leakage 방지

review/2026-04-17/phase_reproducibility_cycle12.md:17:1. **CRITICAL — LOPO oracle 0.341 vs gap 0.265 내부 모순** (ch4_results.tex:415, 428, 448): 본문은 "oracle mean 0.341, generalized 0.032, gap 0.265"라 표기하지만 0.341 - 0.032 = 0.309 ≠ 0.265. CSV 재계산 결과: scoring×family granularity (=11 cells × 11 pathogens 평균) → oracle=0.297, gen=0.032, gap=0.265 (paper의 gap·gen 일치, oracle은 0.297이어야 함). scoring×detector granularity (780 combos) → oracle=0.341, gen=-0.017, gap=0.358. 본문 "0.341"은 detector-level oracle, "gap 0.265"는 family-level gap을 혼용. 3 곳에서 발생. Defense에서 산수 검증 시 즉시 노출.

chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:175:\phantomsection\label{tab:bootstrap_ci}%
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:176:Region-level BCa bootstrap CIs~\cite{efron1987better} (1,000 resamplings, $n = 7$ Spike regions; hereafter \emph{region-level BCa CI}) gave a 95\% CI of [0.323, 0.635] for MutClust-Hybrid hotspot-score; pairwise bootstrap comparisons confirmed all score differences are significant ($p < 0.001$). Two additional BCa CIs reported later in this dissertation use different resampling units and should be interpreted separately: the \emph{combination-level BCa CI} [0.047, 0.202] for the best single scoring--detection combination's mean MCC (Section~\ref{subsec:9pathogen_bootstrap}, 1{,}000 resamples over 11 pathogens) and the \emph{cluster bootstrap CI} [0.195, 0.333] for the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction $\omega^2$ (Section~\ref{subsec:anova_diagnostics}, 1{,}000 cluster resamples over 11 pathogens).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:205:Having confirmed robustness on SARS-CoV-2, the next question is whether the same methods perform well on other pathogens. This section applies the benchmark pipeline to H3N2 and examines structural and phylogenetic aspects that foreshadow the large-scale comparison in Section~\ref{sec:9pathogen_results}.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:207:Application of the benchmark pipeline to Influenza A H3N2 hemagglutinin (1,967 sequences, 5 antigenic sites~\cite{wiley1981structural,wilson1990structural}) revealed that method rankings differ from SARS-CoV-2: MutClust-Fixed outperformed MutClust-Hybrid (HS = 0.661 vs.\ 0.577), because all 543 HA positions have nonzero H-scores, eliminating HDBSCAN's advantage.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:209:Enrichment ratios also decreased (0.87--2.36-fold vs.\ 1.9--23.7-fold for SARS-CoV-2), reflecting the short HA gene and high background mutation rate.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:210:Figure~\ref{fig:cross_pathogen_comparison} directly compares the top-5 scoring-type MCC across all 11 pathogens in Stage~2, illustrating that the optimal scoring type shifts substantially from pathogen to pathogen (e.g., FUBAR pos.\ for SARS-CoV-2, FUBAR Bayes factor for H3N2, homoplasy for Norovirus, EqualWeight for HIV-1 and MERS, pLDDT-inv for RSV, dN/dS for Influenza~B and HCV, stability-based scores for Rabies and EV-A71). This heterogeneity provides direct visual evidence that no universal best method exists across the 11-pathogen panel, complementing the ANOVA interaction effect (Section~\ref{subsec:9pathogen_statistical}) and the LOPO 0/11 match rate (Section~\ref{subsec:9pathogen_lopo}).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:215:\caption{Cross-pathogen MCC comparison across all 11 pathogens (top 5 scoring types per pathogen). The highest-MCC scoring type varies substantially by pathogen, providing direct visual evidence for pathogen-adaptive selection.}
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:230:\textbf{Cross-pathogen summary.} Method rankings differ between SARS-CoV-2 and H3N2, and phylogenetic non-independence analysis reveals that H-score conflates founder effects with positive selection ($\rho = -0.876$). These findings---that the best method is pathogen-dependent and that frequency-based scoring has fundamental limitations---motivate the large-scale cross-pathogen benchmark with expanded information types.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:242:The benchmark evaluates \textbf{20 scoring types} (organized into 6 categories; see Table~\ref{tab:scoring_types} in Chapter~\ref{ch:mutbench}) combined with \textbf{14 detection method families} spanning 5 categories (threshold-based, signal processing, density/clustering, statistical, and adaptive window) that yield \textbf{39 parameter variants} in total, across \textbf{11 pathogens}, totaling $20 \times 39 \times 11 = \textbf{8{,}580}$ evaluations.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:243:The 20 scoring types are derived from \textbf{10 underlying biological features}; some features generate multiple scoring variants (e.g., frequency yields \textit{freq}, \textit{freq\_with\_indel}, and \textit{rare\_freq}), while composite scorings combine multiple features (e.g., EVEscape composite, EqualWeight).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:245:The information-type analysis in Section~\ref{sec:information_analysis} examines these 10 features across the same 11 pathogens used in the main benchmark.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:247:Stage~2 uses MCC rather than hotspot-score because the stability component (Jaccard-based subsampling reproducibility) requires bootstrap validation that has not been cross-validated across all 11 pathogens with their widely varying alignment lengths (261--1,330 AA) and MSA sizes (530--5,019 unique sequences). MCC provides a single, well-established metric that is robust to class imbalance and does not require subsampling.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:257:A total of 8{,}580 evaluations (20 scoring formulas $\times$ 39 detection parameter variants from 14 families $\times$ 11 pathogens) were conducted.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:258:The 20 scoring formulas span six information categories: frequency-based (freq, rare\_freq, freq\_with\_indel), MSA-derived (entropy, entropy\_with\_indel, homoplasy), phylogenetic (dN/dS proxy, FUBAR posterior probability, FUBAR positive selection, FUBAR Bayes factor), structural (pLDDT inverse, SASA, Grantham distance), AI-based (ESM-2 LLR, Tranception, semantic change, stability, stability\_structural), and composite (EVEscape composite, EqualWeight).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:259:Each evaluation computed MCC, F1, precision, and recall against the 3-layer ground truth (Layer A: convergent evolution positions, Layer B: constrained regions, Layer C: DMS).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:260:DMS Layer~C evaluation was conducted for 6 pathogens (SARS-CoV-2, H3N2, HIV-1, RSV, Rabies, EV-A71) where experimental fitness data are available.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:268:The best scoring--detection combination was selected for each of the 11 pathogens based on MCC, and \textbf{all 11/11 pathogens exhibited distinct best combinations} (Table~\ref{tab:9pathogen_best}).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:272:\caption{Best scoring--detection combination for each of the 11 pathogens (by MCC). All 11 pathogens exhibit unique best combinations spanning 4 of 6 scoring categories, with 9 distinct optimal scoring types.}
