chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:17:\textbf{Contribution 2. Statistical demonstration that the optimal biological information source differs fundamentally across pathogens ($\omega^2_{\text{scoring} \times \text{pathogen}} = 0.296$), with 9 distinct optimal information types across 11 pathogens and no cross-pathogen generalization (LOPO 0/11).}
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:18:Statistical analysis of the large-scale benchmark results across 11 RNA viruses provided, through two primary analyses (the scoring~$\times$~pathogen ANOVA interaction and the vaccine-escape enrichment) and two null-consistent corroborations (LOPO 0/11 and Friedman) on the same 8{,}580-evaluation dataset, consistent evidence that the optimal biological information source is pathogen-dependent.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:19:First, the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$ at 20-type granularity; 95\% cluster-bootstrap CI [0.195, 0.333]; $\omega^2 = 0.103$ at 6-category granularity as a collinearity-robust lower bound) was the largest identified source of variance among modeled terms in the factorial ANOVA, with within-cell residual ($\omega^2 \approx 0.39$) representing unmodeled variation including the three-way interaction (Chapter~\ref{ch:results} Table~\ref{tab:9pathogen_anova}).
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:21:Third, the Friedman test ($p = 0.990$) showed no reliably superior combination across all pathogens, consistent with pathogen-dependent optimality.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:22:Fourth, Leave-One-Pathogen-Out (LOPO) cross-validation yielded a 0/11 agreement result, showing that the optimal information source for one pathogen does not generalize to others.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:24:\textbf{Contribution 3 (two-part).} \textit{(3a) Multi-source integration infrastructure}: a compact 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) captures $\approx$98\% (97.6\%) of the full 10-feature ensemble performance, and EqualWeight integration achieves a statistically significant 4.012-fold H3N2 enrichment ($p = 0.0023$) where single-feature approaches fail. \textit{(3b) Externally-valid vaccine-escape enrichment, anchored on HIV-1}: the Layer-A-disjoint subset of HIV-1 escape positions (37 of 45) yields a direct novel-only enrichment of $7.16\text{--}8.24\times$ (worst-case Bonferroni-adjusted Fisher $p = 5 \times 10^{-12}$); H3N2's 9.36$\times$ is a self-consistency check (69\% Layer~A overlap); SARS-CoV-2 is exploratory after multiple-comparison correction.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:27:Vaccine-escape enrichment analysis across 3 of 11 pathogens (H3N2, SARS-CoV-2, HIV-1; 2{,}340 evaluations; selected for availability of curated antibody-escape annotations) was audited for circularity against the Layer~A ground truth. \textbf{HIV-1 is the cleanest external validation}: its escape set shares only 8 of 45 positions (18\%) with HIV-1 Layer~A, so the 7.19$\times$ enrichment (Bonferroni-adjusted $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$) primarily reflects detection of positions outside the benchmark's training signal. \textbf{H3N2 should be read as a self-consistency check, not external validation}: 20 of 29 H3N2 escape positions (69\%) are in Layer~A, and on the 9 Layer~A-disjoint (novel) escape positions the top combination's enrichment drops to 7.19$\times$ with Fisher $p = 0.132$ (not significant under any correction), so the headline H3N2 9.36$\times$ predominantly re-measures Layer~A performance under a different label rather than discovering new escape positions. \textbf{SARS-CoV-2 is exploratory only}: the 7.63$\times$ nominal enrichment does not survive Bonferroni correction ($p_{\text{adj}} \to 1$), and 60\% of its escape set overlaps Layer~A. The practical-impact claim of Contribution~3 therefore rests on HIV-1 as the primary external validation, with H3N2 and SARS-CoV-2 contributing self-consistency and exploratory evidence respectively.

chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:139:The central result---that the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$; 95\% CI [0.195, 0.333]) is the largest identified modeled variance component, alongside a within-cell residual $\omega^2 \approx 0.39$ that reflects further pathogen-level heterogeneity---empirically supports the algorithm selection principle~\cite{kerschke2019algorithm} and provides evidence that the optimal biological information source is pathogen-dependent.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:141:The concordance between Layer~A benchmark rankings and vaccine escape enrichment is strongest for HIV-1 (7.19$\times$, 82\% of the escape set disjoint from Layer~A; Bonferroni-adjusted $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$), which provides the cleanest external validation; H3N2's headline 9.36$\times$ is largely a self-consistency check given 69\% Layer~A overlap, and SARS-CoV-2's 7.63$\times$ is exploratory (Bonferroni-adjusted $p \to 1$). The benchmark's practical utility for identifying immune evasion positions is therefore established with high confidence only on the Layer~A-disjoint subset exemplified by HIV-1.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:143:These conclusions are bounded by limitations enumerated in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}: the eleven-pathogen scope precludes mixed-effects modeling, a covariate-adjusted (length, positive-rate) variance decomposition has not yet been performed, the LOPO 0/11 result is null-consistent under random-combination permutation, the Layer~A construction is partly literature-curated, the multi-source enrichment claim is statistically anchored by HIV-1, and head-to-head comparison with concurrent benchmarks (ViroGym~\cite{virogym2026}, EVEREST~v3~\cite{gurev2026everest_v3}) remains future work.

chapters/ch4_results.tex:809:0/9의 조합 일치율과 4.9\%의 일반화 비율은 벤치마크의 한계가 아니라 \textbf{핵심 발견}이다. 이 결과는 ``단일 최적 방법''이라는 전제 자체가 성립하지 않음을 정량적으로 입증하며, 병원체 적응적 방법 선택(PAHD)의 필요성에 대한 가장 강력한 경험적 근거를 제공한다. $n=9$는 RNA 바이러스의 주요 대표 병원체를 포괄하며, 표본 크기의 제약에도 불구하고 병원체 간 이질성의 통계적 유의성이 ANOVA($\omega^2 = 0.285$), Friedman($p = 0.0015$), LOPO(0/9 일치) 세 가지 독립적 검정에서 모두 확인되었다.

chapters/ch4_results.tex:893:ESM-LLR과 MSA 기반 스코어 간 Spearman 상관관계는 병원체별로 상당히 달랐다. Norovirus는 강한 양의 상관($\rho = 0.63$, E*rare 대비, $p < 10^{-60}$)을 보여, ESM-2의 학습된 표현이 해당 병원체에서 엔트로피 기반 스코어링과 유사한 진화적 신호를 포착함을 나타냈다. 반면 HIV-1은 중간 정도의 음의 상관($\rho = -0.35$, $p < 10^{-14}$)을, Influenza~B는 거의 무상관($\rho = -0.04$, $p = 0.34$)을 보였다. H3N2에서 ESM-LLR은 DMS 적합도 데이터와 양의 상관($\rho = 0.47$, $p < 10^{-30}$)을 보여, 단백질 언어 모델이 실험적으로 측정 가능한 변이 내성을 포착함을 시사하였다. 이러한 결과는 ESM-LLR이 대부분의 병원체에 대해 진정으로 독립적인 스코어링 신호를 제공함을 확인하며, 벤치마크 프레임워크에 대한 교차 패러다임 검증으로서의 사용을 뒷받침한다.

chapters/ch4_results.tex:1107:앞선 절에서 최적의 스코어링--탐지 조합이 병원체마다 다르다는 것을 확인하였다($\omega^2_{\text{family}\times\text{pathogen}} = 0.285$). 이 절에서는 스코어링 공식의 기반이 되는 개별 정보 유형(feature)의 판별력을 분석하여, 교차 병원체 이질성의 원인을 규명한다.

470	\label{subsec:9pathogen_supplementary}
   471	
   472	Several supplementary analyses were conducted to validate the robustness and generalizability of the benchmark findings.
   473	
   474	\textbf{Cross-Paradigm Validation: Protein Language Model Scoring.}
   475	\label{subsec:esm_validation}
   476	To test whether the benchmark findings generalize beyond MSA-derived scoring formulas, an independent scoring paradigm was evaluated: the ESM-2 protein language model (650M parameters)~\cite{lin2023esm2}. ESM-2 computes per-position log-likelihood ratios (ESM-LLR) from a single consensus sequence using learned evolutionary representations, requiring no multiple sequence alignment. This provides orthogonal validation of the benchmark framework because the scoring signal originates from a fundamentally different methodology---a deep neural network trained on millions of protein families---rather than from the same MSA used by the other scoring formulas.
   477	
   478	The 650M-parameter ESM-2 model was selected as it represents the largest single-GPU model in the ESM-2 family, balancing computational feasibility with representation capacity. Larger models (ESM-2 3B) require multi-GPU inference, while smaller models (8M, 35M) may lack sufficient capacity for proteins exceeding 1,000 residues.
   479	ESM-LLR was computed for all 11 pathogens using wild-type marginal scoring: a single forward pass through the model yields $\text{ESM-LLR}[i] = -\log P(a_i \mid \text{context})$, where $a_i$ is the consensus amino acid at position $i$. For proteins exceeding the 1,022-token context window (SARS-CoV-2 Spike: 1,259 AA after MSA trimming; MERS Spike: 1,330 AA), a sliding window with 256-residue overlap was applied and scores were averaged in overlap regions. The resulting ESM-LLR arrays were evaluated through the same 39 detection methods used in the main benchmark.
   480	
   481	In the full 20-scoring benchmark, ESM-2 LLR achieves the best MCC for RSV (0.196) and ranks among the top 3 for SARS-CoV-2, but performs poorly for Norovirus and HIV-1, reinforcing the central finding that no single scoring paradigm dominates across all pathogens. Spearman correlation between ESM-LLR and MSA-based scores varies substantially: Norovirus shows strong positive correlation ($\rho = 0.63$, $p < 10^{-60}$), while HIV-1 shows moderate negative correlation ($\rho = -0.35$, $p < 10^{-14}$), confirming that ESM-2 provides a genuinely independent scoring signal for most pathogens.
   482	
   483	\textbf{ANOVA Diagnostic Tests.}
   484	\label{subsec:anova_diagnostics}
   485	The Shapiro-Wilk test on ANOVA residuals rejected normality ($W = 0.974$, $p < 10^{-29}$), and Levene's test rejected homoscedasticity for all factors.
   486	However, the non-normality is mild (residual skewness = 0.14, excess kurtosis = 2.83), and the large sample size ($N = 8{,}580$) ensures ANOVA robustness.
   487	A limitation of this design is that the 39 parameter variants within each (scoring, detection family, pathogen) cell are not fully independent, sharing the same input MSA and ground truth; the effective number of independent units is closer to the number of unique cells ($20 \times 14 \times 11 = 3{,}080$) than $N = 8{,}580$.
   488	The $\omega^2$ estimates should therefore be interpreted as indicative effect sizes rather than precise variance decompositions. The cluster bootstrap reported below is explicitly the effective-$N$-aware correction: resampling is performed \emph{at the pathogen level} (11 independent clusters) rather than at the evaluation level ($N = 8{,}580$), which naturally absorbs the within-pathogen dependence. Specifically, 1{,}000 cluster-bootstrap resamples over the 11 pathogens yield a 95\% CI of $[0.195, 0.333]$ for the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction; this CI width (0.138) already reflects the effective-$N$ contraction and does not require an additional $\sqrt{N/N_{\text{eff}}}$ correction.
   489	For sensitivity, a naive $N = 8{,}580$ bootstrap (ignoring pathogen-cluster structure) yields a narrower CI of $[0.260, 0.321]$; the wider cluster-bootstrap CI is the more honest reference for inference about the pathogen-dependence conclusion. The effect remains above Cohen's large-effect threshold ($\omega^2 > 0.14$) under both bootstrap schemes and at the more conservative 6-category aggregation. The 11-cluster regime is below the rule-of-thumb $\geq 30$ for percentile-bootstrap CI calibration; a wild-cluster bootstrap (Cameron, Gelbach \& Miller 2008) is the standard sharper alternative for $G \leq 30$ and is recommended for any future cycle that revises the headline interval. For the present cycle the percentile interval is reported with the explicit caveat that small-cluster coverage may be slightly anticonservative; the lower bound (0.195) sits well above Cohen's large threshold even under generous coverage adjustment.
   490	A sensitivity analysis excluding HCV---whose Layer~A is based on hypervariable regions (diversifying selection) rather than convergent evolution---yields $\omega^2_{\text{scoring} \times \text{pathogen}} = 0.246$, confirming that the interaction effect is not attributable to HCV's atypical ground truth definition.
   491	Kruskal-Wallis non-parametric tests confirmed all effects (pathogen: $H = 1{,}120.8$, $p < 10^{-234}$; detection family: $H = 129.1$, $p < 10^{-21}$; scoring: $H = 277.9$, $p < 10^{-47}$), maintaining the reliability of the directional ANOVA conclusions despite these caveats.
   492	
   493	\textbf{Precision@$k$ Analysis.}
   494	\label{subsec:precision_at_k}
   495	The detection precision and recall of the best combination for each pathogen were analyzed. Table~\ref{tab:precision_at_k} presents the precision, recall, detection size, and best MCC for the top-1 combination of each pathogen.

   557	\subsection{Summary of Key Findings}
   558	\label{subsec:pahd_motivation_summary}
   559	
   560	The cross-pathogen benchmark supports pathogen-adaptive method selection through two primary analyses (scoring~$\times$~pathogen $\omega^2$ interaction and vaccine-escape cross-validation) plus two null-consistent corroborations (LOPO 0/11 and Friedman). The four lenses re-parameterize the same dataset and are not independent replications.
   561	
   562	\begin{enumerate}
   563	\item \textbf{Interaction dominance (modeled)}: Among the modeled factors, the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$; 95\% cluster-bootstrap CI [0.195, 0.333]) is the largest component, exceeding all main effects and other two-way interactions; a within-cell residual $\omega^2 \approx 0.39$ captures the unmodeled three-way interaction and parameter-variant noise. The optimal information source is pathogen-dependent.
   564	\item \textbf{Unique best combinations}: 11 unique best combinations were observed across 11/11 pathogens, with 9 distinct scoring types. No two pathogens share the same best combination.
   565	\item \textbf{Generalization failure}: LOPO cross-validation yielded 0/11 combination matches with a mean generalization MCC of 0.032. The best combination selected from training pathogens does not generalize to new pathogens.
   566	\item \textbf{No universally superior combination}: Friedman $\chi^2 = 7.69$, $p = 0.990$. No single combination is reliably distinguishable as superior across all pathogens.
   567	\end{enumerate}
   568	
   569	Together, the four lenses provide consistent evidence that the best-performing method differs by pathogen and that the scoring~$\times$~pathogen interaction is the largest modeled variance component. The next section investigates \textit{why} this interaction arises by analysing individual information types.

   151	The mean oracle recall across 11 pathogens is 0.552 (Table~\ref{tab:precision_at_k}), indicating that the best combination for each pathogen detects approximately half of the known convergent evolution positions. While this may appear insufficient for safety-critical applications, three observations provide context.
   152	
   153	First, \textit{the missed positions are not randomly distributed}. Positions with low recall tend to be those where the convergent evolution signal is weakest---positions documented in only 3 lineages (the minimum threshold for Layer~A inclusion), or positions where the selective advantage is epistatic (dependent on other mutations) rather than individually strong. For SARS-CoV-2, the 8 undetected Layer~A positions (recall = 0.680, 17/25 detected) are predominantly NTD supersite positions where immune evasion operates through conformational changes rather than direct frequency elevation.
   154	
   155	Second, \textit{multi-source integration recovers positions missed by single-information approaches}. For H3N2, frequency-based scoring misses antigenic site~B positions (155, 159, 160) that are structurally constrained, but the EqualWeight ensemble captures them through the pLDDT and homoplasy components (Section~\ref{subsec:search_space_reduction}). This complementarity---where different information types detect different subsets of positions---is the mechanistic basis for the dominant scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction.
   156	
   157	Third, \textit{region-level coverage is substantially higher than position-level recall}. Under $\pm$10 position windows (approximately one epitope width), the mean MCC increases from 0.341 to 0.454, and Influenza~B reaches 0.924. Positions scored as ``missed'' in exact evaluation are often detected within 1--2 residues of the true position---close enough to guide experimental prioritization, which is the practical goal.
   158	
   159	The primary risk of missed positions lies in pathogens with low recall: EV-A71 (recall = 0.185) and Rabies (recall = 0.308). For these pathogens, the 261~AA and 491~AA post-truncation alignment lengths provide limited statistical power, and the small number of detected positions ($n = 10$ and $n = 39$, respectively) may not adequately represent the full landscape of adaptive sites. Users applying MutBench to such short-protein pathogens should interpret the detected positions as a prioritized subset rather than an exhaustive list, and complement computational detection with experimental validation (DMS or epitope mapping).

   193	\subsection{Cross-Validation via Vaccine Escape Enrichment}
   194	\label{sec:cross_validation_escape}
   195	
   196	A critical question for any benchmark is whether its rankings reflect genuine biological relevance or merely circular evaluation artifacts.
   197	The vaccine escape enrichment analysis across three pathogens (2{,}340 evaluations) provides \emph{partial} cross-validation of the Layer~A benchmark results, with the strength of external validation differing substantially by pathogen.
   198	
   199	\paragraph{Three-tier evidence rule.} Pathogens are assigned to one of three evidence tiers using two operational criteria evaluated jointly: (i)~\emph{Bonferroni survival} of the Fisher's exact $p$-value across 780 scoring--detection combinations ($p_{\text{adj}} < 0.05$), and (ii)~\emph{Layer~A independence}, defined as fewer than one-third of escape positions overlapping the pathogen's Layer~A set ($|\text{escape} \cap \text{Layer A}| / |\text{escape}| < 33\%$). A pathogen passing both criteria is classified as a \textbf{primary external anchor} (HIV-1: 18\% overlap, $p_{\text{adj}} = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$); a pathogen passing only (i)~is a \textbf{self-consistency check} (H3N2: 69\% overlap, $p_{\text{adj}} = 2.6 \times 10^{-5}$); a pathogen passing neither is reported as \textbf{exploratory} (SARS-CoV-2: $p_{\text{adj}} > 0.05$). The 33\% overlap threshold separates the three observed pathogens into distinct tiers without intermediate values; sensitivity to the threshold (25\%, 33\%, 50\%) does not change tier assignments for these three cases. With only three pathogens any threshold in $(18\%, 60\%)$ produces the same partition; the rule is therefore calibrated on observed data and explicitly underpowered as a *predictive* rule for new pathogens. Future cycles with additional escape-annotated pathogens will test whether the 33\% threshold remains the correct cut-point; the present work uses it as a transparent decision rule, not a generalised threshold.
   200	
   201	HIV-1 is the cleanest external validation: its escape set shares only 8 of 45 positions (18\%) with HIV-1 Layer~A, so the 7.19$\times$ enrichment (Bonferroni-adjusted $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$) primarily reflects detection of positions outside the benchmark's training signal. A direct novel-only re-test on the 37 Layer~A-disjoint positions (best combination freq~$+$~Wavelet~$t = 1.5$) yields enrichment in the range $7.16\text{--}8.24\times$ depending on how many of the 8 escape~$\cap$~Layer-A positions the detector also captures (sensitivity $k \in \{0, \ldots, 8\}$); even the conservative worst case ($k = 8$, all overlap positions detected) gives $7.16\times$ with Fisher $p = 5.0 \times 10^{-12}$, which survives Bonferroni correction ($\times 780$) by more than nine orders of magnitude.
   202	In contrast, H3N2's 9.36$\times$ is largely a self-consistency check: 20 of 29 escape positions (69\%) already lie in H3N2 Layer~A, so the high enrichment predominantly re-measures Layer~A performance. Restricting the calculation to the 9 Layer~A-disjoint (novel) escape positions drops the enrichment to 7.19$\times$ with Fisher $p = 0.132$ (not significant; Chapter~\ref{ch:results} Table~\ref{tab:vaccine_escape_stage3} circularity audit).
   203	SARS-CoV-2's 7.63$\times$ nominal enrichment does not survive Bonferroni correction and is reported as exploratory only.
   204	
   205	The benchmark is \emph{not a circular artifact} in the algorithmic sense (ground truth and scoring are computed independently), but the practical-value claim of Contribution~3 is carried primarily by HIV-1, with H3N2 and SARS-CoV-2 contributing self-consistency and exploratory evidence.
   206	
   207	\textbf{Concurrent-benchmark task-orthogonality.} The MutBench panel overlaps with ViroGym (HIV, SARS-CoV-2, H3N2 are common) and EVEREST~v3 (HIV, SARS-CoV-2 forecasting clades), so a head-to-head leaderboard appears feasible in principle. We do not run one in this dissertation because the metric universes are structurally non-overlapping: ViroGym and EVEREST optimise per-variant fitness Spearman against DMS, while MutBench optimises per-region binary MCC against the 3-layer ground truth; converting between the two requires either (a) thresholding fitness predictions at a top-$k$ cutoff to obtain a binary region call (which throws away the continuous information ViroGym/EVEREST were optimised for), or (b) summarising MutBench detections into a fitness ranking (which throws away the spatial-clustering information MutBench was optimised for). Either reduction biases the comparison toward the receiving format. The principled task-aligned subset evaluation (binarise fitness predictions at top-$k$ thresholds matched to MutBench's positive-rate per pathogen, then compare MCC on the shared HIV/SARS-CoV-2/H3N2 panel) is queued as a defense-week sprint item (Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion} Table~\ref{tab:limitations_summary}); the present cycle's contribution is the *structural orthogonality argument* itself, which removes the head-to-head as a knock-down objection.
   208	
   209	This cross-validation is particularly important for the five pathogens without DMS data (Layer~C), where benchmark validity rests primarily on Layer~A.
   210	The EVEREST study and its v3 expansion~\cite{gurev2025everest,gurev2026everest_v3} demonstrate that even with 45 DMS datasets, current models fail to reliably predict mutations in over half of the 40 WHO priority RNA viruses, with reliability worst for surface glycoproteins---an external finding that independently corroborates the LOPO 0/11 non-transferability reported in Chapter~\ref{ch:results}. For H3N2 specifically, the antigenic-cartography lineage of Smith et al.~\cite{smith2004antigenic} and the recent PLM-based extensions of PLANT~\cite{plant2025antigenic} and Shah et al.~\cite{shah2024h3n2ml} target a prediction task complementary to MutBench's region-level detection; the 69\% Layer~A overlap reported above should therefore be interpreted as task-internal self-consistency rather than as a head-to-head antigenic-prediction claim.
   211	MutBench's combination of Layer~A benchmark rankings with independent vaccine escape validation provides complementary evidence that circumvents DMS data availability constraints, supporting the validity of Layer~A as a ground truth even for pathogens where DMS data are unavailable.

   214	\subsection{Practical Considerations for Public Health Surveillance}
   215	\label{sec:practical_surveillance}
   216	
   217	Given SARS-CoV-2's generation time ({$\sim$}5 days) and sequence submission delay ({$\sim$}14 days), a minimum 4-week window is required for real-time TC-freq alerts. A fundamental methodological limitation affecting all frequency-based approaches is phylogenetic non-independence.
   218	
   219	For public health practitioners, MutBench results can be operationalized through the following workflow when a novel pathogen or variant emerges: (1)~compute the 20 scoring types from the available MSA (requiring only sequence data and publicly available tools: MAFFT for alignment, HyPhy for FUBAR, ESM-2 for PLM scores, AlphaFold2 for structural features); (2)~if the pathogen belongs to a family already represented in MutBench (e.g., Coronaviridae, Orthomyxoviridae, Flaviviridae), use the family-level scoring recommendation from Table~\ref{tab:scoring_recommendation} as a starting point; (3)~if the pathogen is novel, apply the EqualWeight ensemble as a conservative baseline, which achieves 98\% of full-feature performance with only 4 core features (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency). This workflow integrates with existing surveillance platforms such as Nextstrain~\cite{nextstrain2018hadfield} and GISAID~\cite{shu2017gisaid}, which already provide the MSA inputs required by MutBench.

   846	\subsection{Practical Validation: Search Space Reduction}
   847	\label{subsec:search_space_reduction}
   848	
   849	The analysis results above demonstrate that multiple information types contribute to hotspot prediction, but the most informative feature differs by pathogen. This subsection evaluates whether integrating all 10 features reduces the experimental search space for hotspot validation.
   850	
   851	The integration method uses equal-weight combination: each feature is z-score normalized across all $L$ alignment positions, directional signs are applied (to handle inverse associations such as pLDDT AUC $< 0.5$ for MERS), and the weighted combination $s_i = \sum_{f=1}^{10} (1/10) \cdot \mathrm{sign}(\hat{s}_f) \cdot z_{i,f}$ is computed. Positions exceeding a percentile threshold are called as hotspots. Equal weighting was chosen because, with only 11 reference pathogens, adaptive weighting strategies introduce more noise than signal (see below).
   852	
   853	Leave-One-Pathogen-Out (LOPO) cross-validation was conducted across all 11 pathogens, comparing EqualWeight against frequency-only (FreqThresh) and random baselines.
   854	Under the EqualWeight top-10\% threshold, mean MCC = 0.083 (9/11 pathogens positive), outperforming FreqThresh (0.075, 8/11 positive) and random (0.000, 5/11 positive).
   855	
   856	\textbf{Vaccine escape position validation.}
   857	To assess practical relevance, the 20 scoring $\times$ 39 detector combinations were evaluated against experimentally confirmed vaccine/antibody escape positions for 3 pathogens: H3N2 (29 antigenic drift sites in HA sites~A and~B), SARS-CoV-2 (30 Spike escape sites in RBD, NTD, and S2), and HIV-1 (45 Env gp120 antibody escape sites). A total of 2,340 enrichment evaluations were performed (Table~\ref{tab:vaccine_escape_stage3}). Enrichment is defined as
   858	\[
   859	E = \frac{\text{observed overlap}}{\text{expected overlap}} = \frac{|D \cap A|}{|D|\,|A|/L},
   860	\]
   861	where $D$ is the set of detected hotspot positions, $A$ is the set of annotated escape positions, and $L$ is the protein length. Significance is tested by Fisher's exact test on the $2 \times 2$ table $\{|D \cap A|,\;|D \setminus A|,\;|A \setminus D|,\;L - |D \cup A|\}$. These three pathogens were selected on the single criterion of availability of curated antibody-escape annotations at the time of analysis; the remaining 8 pathogens are not included because comparable escape-position databases were not available.

Under Bonferroni correction across the 780-test selection ($p_{\text{adj}} = \min(1,\,780 \times p)$): H3N2 FUBAR+Wavelet $p_{\text{nominal}} = 3.37 \times 10^{-8}$, $p_{\text{adj}} = 2.63 \times 10^{-5}$ (survives); HIV-1 freq+Wavelet $p_{\text{nominal}} = 3.16 \times 10^{-19}$, $p_{\text{adj}} = 2.47 \times 10^{-16}$ (survives, overwhelming); SARS-CoV-2 FUBAR+FreqThresh $p_{\text{nominal}} = 0.026$, $p_{\text{adj}} \to 1.00$ (does not survive; exploratory only). \textbf{Novel-only enrichment} (restricting the escape set to positions disjoint from the corresponding Layer~A set) is reported in the bottom rows: for H3N2, the novel escape set has 9 of 29 positions (31\%), and the top combination's novel-only enrichment is $7.19\times$ with Fisher $p = 0.132$ (not significant)---i.e., most of the 9.36$\times$ signal reflects re-detection of Layer~A sites rather than discovery of new escape positions. For HIV-1, the novel escape set has 37 of 45 positions (82\%), and a direct novel-only re-test on freq~$+$~Wavelet~$t = 1.5$ yields enrichment $7.16\text{--}8.24\times$ (sensitivity to $k = 0, \ldots, 8$ detected positions inside the escape~$\cap$~Layer-A overlap; worst case $7.16\times$, Fisher $p = 5.0 \times 10^{-12}$, surviving Bonferroni by $>$9 orders of magnitude). HIV-1 is therefore the cleanest external validation under any sensitivity assumption. For SARS-CoV-2, the novel escape set has 12 of 30 positions (40\%); novel-only enrichment is not interpretable given the overall nominal $p = 0.026$. \textbf{Winner's-curse context}: among the $k$ Bonferroni-surviving combinations per pathogen (H3N2: $k = 67$; HIV-1: $k = 132$; SARS-CoV-2: $k = 29$), the \emph{mean} surviving enrichment is materially lower than the top-1 value (H3N2 mean $\approx 4.7\times$; HIV-1 mean $\approx 4\text{--}5\times$), so the headline top-1 enrichments should be read as upper-envelope estimates, not typical values. \textbf{$\alpha$-sensitivity}: tightening $\alpha$ from $0.05$ to $0.01$ does not change tier assignments---HIV-1 ($p_{\text{adj}} = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$) and H3N2 ($p_{\text{adj}} = 2.6 \times 10^{-5}$) remain Bonferroni-significant by $>$10 orders of magnitude; SARS-CoV-2 ($p_{\text{adj}} \to 1$) remains non-surviving; the three-tier rule (Section~\ref{sec:cross_validation_escape}) is therefore robust to the conventional $\alpha \in \{0.05, 0.01\}$ choice. \textbf{Cross-pathogen denominator}: extending the per-pathogen Bonferroni denominator to the joint $20 \times 39 \times 11 = 8{,}580$-test family (HIV-1 $p_{\text{adj}} \approx 2.7 \times 10^{-15}$, H3N2 $p_{\text{adj}} \approx 2.9 \times 10^{-4}$) does not change tier assignments either, and the Holm-Bonferroni step-down or Benjamini-Hochberg FDR alternatives would only relax these bounds; the per-pathogen 780-denominator is reported as the operationally relevant family because each pathogen is its own selection problem.}

   890	\textbf{Key findings:}
   891	All three pathogens achieve nominally significant vaccine escape enrichment ($p < 0.05$) with the optimal scoring--detection combination; after Bonferroni correction across 780 combinations, H3N2 and HIV-1 survive while SARS-CoV-2 is exploratory only. The best scoring \emph{category} for escape enrichment agrees with the Layer~A benchmark results at the category level (Phylogenetic for H3N2, Frequency for HIV-1), though the top scoring \emph{type} within that category can differ between the two evaluations (HIV-1 Layer~A best is \textit{entropy} with Wavelet(t{=}2.0), MCC 0.275; HIV-1 escape best is \textit{freq} with Wavelet(t{=}1.5), enrichment 7.19$\times$---both frequency-derived and correlated at $\rho \approx 0.97$, Section~\ref{sec:information_analysis}). The strength of this concordance as \emph{external} evidence is pathogen-dependent: HIV-1 provides the cleanest external validation (82\% of its escape set lies outside Layer~A; see circularity audit below), whereas for H3N2 the 69\% Layer~A/escape overlap means that the concordance is largely a self-consistency check rather than independent replication.
   892	
   893	For H3N2, FUBAR Bayes factor captures 9 of 29 antigenic drift sites with 9.36-fold enrichment; 8 of those 9 captured positions are already in Layer~A (the audit paragraph below quantifies the resulting novel-only enrichment of 7.19$\times$ with Fisher $p = 0.132$, not significant). The multi-source EqualWeight integration achieves 4.012-fold enrichment ($p = 0.0023$), capturing positions in both antigenic site~A (position~137) and site~B (positions~155, 159, 160, 186, 188), while frequency alone misses the structurally constrained site~B positions.
   894	
   895	A limitation of this analysis is that vaccine escape validation was feasible for only 3 of 11 pathogens (H3N2, HIV-1, SARS-CoV-2). Table~\ref{tab:escape_availability} summarizes, for each of the remaining 8~pathogens, the escape-data source considered and the specific reason that a position-level validation set could not be constructed under the same protocol (curated antibody-escape positions with residue-level mapping to the benchmark's reference sequence).

   918	The exclusion reasons fall into four categories: (i)~annotation granularity too coarse (Dengue, Influenza~B, Rabies, Norovirus); (ii)~sample size below the $n \geq 15$ threshold adopted for the three included pathogens (MERS, EV-A71); (iii)~confound with the benchmark's Layer~A set (RSV); and (iv)~mechanism mismatch (HCV: drug-resistance, not immune escape). No pathogen was excluded because of an expectation of low enrichment; the decision was made on data-availability grounds prior to running any enrichment computation. The generalizability of the enrichment finding to the other 8~pathogens therefore remains to be established, and the three validated pathogens should be read as a data-availability convenience sample rather than a balanced subset.
   919	
   920	\textbf{Layer~A / escape-list overlap (circularity audit).}
   921	Because Layer~A for H3N2, SARS-CoV-2, and HIV-1 is partly constructed from immune-escape-tagged positions (Chapter~\ref{ch:mutbench}, \texttt{layer\_a\_tags.csv} with an \texttt{immune\_escape} evidence tag), the vaccine-escape validation sets used in this section are not fully disjoint from the Layer~A ground truth. Concretely, the set overlap between the Layer~A immune-escape subset and the vaccine-escape validation list is 20/29 for H3N2 (69\% of the escape list is already in Layer~A), 18/30 for SARS-CoV-2 (60\%), and 8/45 for HIV-1 (18\%). A scoring method that excels on Layer~A therefore has a built-in advantage on H3N2 and SARS-CoV-2 escape enrichment, and the 9.36$\times$/7.63$\times$ values should be read as a self-consistency check rather than an independent replication on those two pathogens. HIV-1's 7.19$\times$ is the least affected by this circularity because 37 of 45 escape positions (82\%) are outside Layer~A and are genuinely novel relative to the benchmark ground truth. The qualitative conclusion---that benchmark-optimal scoring also best captures escape positions---holds, but the quantitative enrichment values for H3N2 and SARS-CoV-2 must be interpreted with this overlap in mind.
   922	
   923	\textbf{Search space reduction.}
   924	For a typical viral protein of 500 positions, the optimal scoring--detection combination narrows the candidate list to 20--80 positions with 7--9-fold enrichment for escape sites. This transforms hotspot detection from an exhaustive search into a guided investigation, providing a ranked candidate list that directs limited experimental resources toward the most promising positions.

   927	\subsection{Adaptive Weighting: Current Limits and Future Potential}
   928	\label{subsec:adaptive_weighting_limits}
   929	
   930	Three adaptive weighting strategies were evaluated against the equal-weight baseline: kNN-weighted ($k{=}3$ inverse-distance interpolation of RF importance weights using a 13-dimensional pathogen profile), Top-3 AUC (equal weight on 3 highest-AUC features from nearest neighbors), and Correlation-aware ensemble (equal weight on 5 lowest-correlation features with AUC $> 0.5$).
   931	All adaptive strategies performed worse than EqualWeight: kNN-weighted achieved a maximum mean MCC of 0.020, Top-3 AUC 0.049, and Correlation-aware 0.043, compared to EqualWeight's 0.083.
   932	
   933	This underperformance is explained by the sparsity of the reference database.
   934	With only 11 reference pathogens (10 available in each LOPO fold), the 13-dimensional pathogen profile space is severely undersampled (dimensions-to-samples ratio $\approx 1.1$), making $k$NN matching unreliable and introducing noise rather than adaptation.
   935	
   936	However, the oracle strategy (mean MCC = 0.160) approximately doubles EqualWeight performance (0.083), confirming that per-pathogen weighting provides genuine improvement when labeled data is available.
   937	Closing this gap without labels requires expanding the reference database to 20--30+ pathogens for meaningful $k$NN matching in the pathogen profile space.
   938	This is a finding about the current state of available data, not a failure of the adaptive concept; the oracle ceiling demonstrates that the potential for adaptive improvement exists and motivates knowledge base expansion as a concrete future direction.
   939

   941	\subsection{Information-Type Analysis Summary}
   942	\label{subsec:info_analysis_summary}
   943	
   944	The multi-source information integration analysis yields four key findings:
   945	
   946	\begin{itemize}
   947	\item \textbf{Feature heterogeneity}: The most discriminative information type differs across pathogens (5~distinct best features among 11 pathogens), providing a mechanistic explanation for the scoring$\,\times\,$pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$) observed in the ANOVA.
   948	\item \textbf{Compact core}: A 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) captures $\approx$98\% (97.6\%) of the full 10-feature ensemble performance under uniform weighting, while features that are noise on average (ESM-2, SASA) are the best discriminators for specific pathogens.
   949	\item \textbf{Practical search space reduction}: Equal-weight 10-feature integration achieves statistically significant H3N2 vaccine escape enrichment (4.012$\times$, $p = 0.0023$) where single-feature approaches fail to reach significance, transforming exhaustive experimental screening into guided investigation.
   950	\item \textbf{Adaptive weighting potential}: The oracle ceiling (MCC = 0.160 vs.\ EqualWeight 0.083) confirms that per-pathogen feature weighting can double performance, but requires expanding the reference database beyond the current 11 pathogens.
   951	\end{itemize}

   954	\noindent\textbf{Chapter summary.}
   955	This chapter reported the experimental results of MutBench in five sections.
   956	Stage~1 validated the framework on SARS-CoV-2: MutClust-Hybrid achieved hotspot-score 0.778 on synthetic data, though real GISAID data showed F1 = 0.123 while maintaining biological validity (enrichment $>$ 6.9-fold).
   957	Stage~2 extended evaluation to all 11 pathogens (8,580 evaluations), revealing that the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$; 95\% CI [0.195, 0.333]) is the largest modeled variance component (within-cell residual $\omega^2 \approx 0.39$), with LOPO cross-validation yielding 0/11 exact matches and a 0.265 MCC oracle-vs-generalized gap, and Friedman test showing no reliably superior combination ($p = 0.990$).
   958	The information-type analysis identified a 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) capturing $\approx$98\% (97.6\%) of full ensemble performance. Vaccine escape cross-validation was carried primarily by HIV-1 (7.19$\times$, 82\% of escape set disjoint from Layer~A; Bonferroni-adjusted $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$); H3N2's 9.36$\times$ is largely a self-consistency check (69\% Layer~A overlap; novel-only enrichment 7.19$\times$, $p = 0.132$), and SARS-CoV-2 is exploratory after multiple-comparison correction.
   959	The broader implications for adaptive method selection, including knowledge base scaling requirements and future extensions, are discussed in Chapter~\ref{ch:discussion}.

chapters_en/ch1_introduction.tex:33:Existing computational approaches for hotspot detection have relied predominantly on two types of information: mutation frequency and Shannon entropy. While these capture the most direct signals of mutational enrichment, they fail to distinguish biologically meaningful hotspots from founder-effect artifacts and cannot leverage the growing wealth of complementary information sources---including phylogenetic selection signals, protein language model predictions, structural features, and deep mutational scanning data. Concurrent benchmarks evaluate per-variant fitness regression on overlapping virus panels (notably ViroGym~\cite{virogym2026}, 13 viruses / 79 DMS / 7 phenotypes; EVEREST~v3~\cite{gurev2026everest_v3}, 45 DMS / 31 forecasting clades / 40 WHO priority viruses; ProteinGym~\cite{notin2023proteingym,notin2025proteingym_v13}, 217 DMS / 90+ baselines), but none has performed a region-level hotspot-detection comparison that systematically decomposes which biological information types are most effective for which pathogens, leaving researchers to default to frequency-based approaches regardless of the virus under study.
chapters_en/ch1_introduction.tex:38:Current viral genomics platforms such as Nextstrain~\cite{nextstrain2018hadfield} and PANGO lineage classification~\cite{rambaut2020pangolin} monitor variant emergence but do not provide systematic evaluation of which biological information sources are most effective for hotspot detection.
chapters_en/ch1_introduction.tex:42:In the first stage (\textit{sequence collection}), viral genomes from infected individuals are sequenced over weeks to months at research institutions worldwide and deposited in public databases such as GISAID and NCBI GenBank; for SARS-CoV-2, millions of sequences have been accumulated since 2020, while for influenza, tens of thousands of sequences span several decades.
chapters_en/ch1_introduction.tex:46:In the third stage (\textit{experimental validation}), the computationally identified hotspot candidates are individually verified through laboratory experiments such as Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS), neutralization assays, and cell infection assays.
chapters_en/ch1_introduction.tex:47:Because each experimental validation requires weeks to months per position, it is prohibitively resource-intensive to test all positions; computational analysis therefore serves as a critical filter that prioritizes positions for experimental investigation.

chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:276:\caption{3-Layer Ground Truth Framework. Layer~A (convergent evolution) defines true positives for MCC computation, Layer~B (purifying selection) defines true negatives for constrained FPR, and Layer~C (DMS fitness) provides independent experimental validation. The three layers capture orthogonal dimensions of mutational importance.}
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:283:Layer~B asks ``is this position structurally constrained?'' (a \textit{structural} question), identifying positions where any mutation destroys protein function.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:284:Layer~C asks ``what is the measurable functional impact of mutations at this position?'' (a \textit{functional} question), using laboratory DMS experiments that directly quantify how each amino acid substitution affects viral fitness (e.g., cell entry efficiency, receptor binding affinity).
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:285:This separation means each layer provides an independent, non-redundant perspective: Layer~A captures evolutionary signals that DMS cannot (multi-lineage emergence patterns require years of surveillance data), while Layer~C captures functional effects that convergent evolution analysis cannot (a position may have strong fitness effects but not yet show convergent evolution if the virus has not encountered sufficient selection pressure).
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:300:\subsubsection{Layer B: Constrained Purifying Selection}
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:303:These are positions where mutations are actively \textit{removed} from the viral population because they destroy protein folding, disrupt membrane fusion, or abolish receptor binding---any mutation here is lethal or severely deleterious to the virus.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:306:When detection methods incorrectly identify these positions as hotspots, they are counted as false positives, and the constrained false positive rate (constrained FPR) is computed.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:309:Layer~B positions were identified based on two types of evidence from the cited literature: (1)~structural essentiality---positions within domains whose disruption abolishes protein function (e.g., fusion peptide, HR1/HR2 heptad repeats, structural disulfide-bonding cysteine residues), as determined by published mutagenesis or structural studies; and (2)~evolutionary conservation---positions exhibiting dN/dS $< 0.5$ across diverse viral isolates, indicating strong purifying selection against amino acid changes. The 0.5 threshold follows the convention used in comparative genomics for identifying purifying selection~\cite{yang2007paml}, where $\omega < 1$ indicates purifying selection and values below 0.5 represent particularly strong functional constraint.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:313:\subsubsection{Layer C: DMS Experimental Validation}
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:315:For six pathogens with available Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS) experimental data---SARS-CoV-2~\cite{dadonaite2023dms}, H3N2, HIV-1, RSV, Rabies, and EV-A71---experimentally measured fitness effects are used as ground truth.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:316:Unlike Layer~A (which infers importance from evolutionary patterns) and Layer~B (which infers importance from structural conservation), Layer~C provides direct experimental measurements: in DMS experiments, every possible single amino acid substitution at every position is physically constructed in the laboratory, and its effect on a quantifiable phenotype (e.g., cell entry efficiency for SARS-CoV-2, replicative fitness for H3N2) is measured.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:317:Positions in the top 20\% of mean absolute fitness effect from DMS data are classified as functionally important positions, and the DMS F1 score is computed against detection results. The 20\% threshold was chosen to balance sensitivity and specificity: it captures positions with substantial fitness effects while maintaining sufficient contrast with non-functional positions. Sensitivity analysis (Section~\ref{subsec:dms_evolution_correlation}) confirmed that Layer~C rankings remain stable across thresholds from 15\% to 25\%.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:319:The DMS phenotypes measured differ by pathogen: cell entry fitness for SARS-CoV-2~\cite{dadonaite2024nature} and RSV~\cite{simonich2026rsvdms}, viral replicative fitness for H3N2~\cite{lee2018h3n2dms}, viral growth in cell culture for HIV-1~\cite{haddox2018hiv1dms}, G-protein-mediated cell entry for Rabies~\cite{aditham2025rabies}, and replicative fitness for EV-A71~\cite{bakhache2025eva71}. Table~\ref{tab:dms_preprocessing} summarises the per-pathogen DMS preprocessing conventions adopted in this benchmark; cell-line and replicate-aggregation choices follow the released-source defaults except where noted.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:323:\caption{DMS preprocessing conventions per Layer~C source. ``Mean abs.\ effect'' refers to the per-position mean absolute fitness effect across all amino-acid substitutions, used as the score from which the top-20\% threshold defines Layer~C positives. All sources used the released processed-fitness tables; raw read filtering and replicate aggregation follow each source's published default unless noted.}
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:348:This occurs because these residues are simultaneously under immune evasion pressure (positive selection) and structural constraints (purifying selection), representing dual-selection sites.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:353:Layer~A (convergent evolution) and Layer~C (DMS fitness) can disagree at individual positions: a residue may show convergent evolution in the phylogeny (Layer~A positive) but have low DMS fitness cost (Layer~C negative), or vice versa. This does not require a merged classification decision because the two layers feed \textit{different} evaluation metrics under non-overlapping scopes:
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:355:(2)~\textbf{Layer~C $\to$ DMS F1}: Layer~C top-20\% positions are treated as positives (for 6 pathogens with DMS); Layer~A membership does not affect the DMS F1 calculation.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:357:Thus a position that is Layer~A-positive but Layer~C-negative counts as a true positive for the MCC metric (it is evolutionarily hot by construction) and a true negative for the DMS F1 metric (it is not among the top 20\% of measured fitness effects) simultaneously, without internal contradiction. This is consistent with the design choice that no single universal ``hotspot'' label is asserted; rather, the benchmark reports performance against each operationalization of hotspot-ness independently.

chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:388:``---'' indicates that no DMS data is available for that pathogen.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:397:Norovirus, Dengue, Influenza~B, MERS, and HCV lack Layer~C (DMS data).
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:399:(2)~restricting the benchmark to six pathogens would provide insufficient statistical power for the cross-pathogen analyses (ANOVA, Friedman, LOPO) in Chapter~\ref{ch:results};
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:400:and (3)~including pathogens with diverse evolutionary dynamics and varying ground truth availability more accurately reflects real-world conditions where comprehensive ground truth is rarely available for all pathogens.

chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:425:\textbf{DMS-based functional sites.}\phantomsection\label{subsec:dms_ground_truth}
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:426:The DMS fitness data are derived from the full-length Spike protein characterization experiment by Dadonaite et al.~\cite{dadonaite2023dms, dadonaite2024nature}.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:436:\textbf{Synthetic data (controlled signal recovery test).}
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:437:The synthetic benchmark was designed as a controlled signal recovery test that evaluates how accurately each detection method recovers artificially inserted signals at known positions.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:439:High H-scores (0.8--1.2) are assigned to Core Candidate Mutation (CCM) seed positions (AA 484, 501, 417, 452---the four Spike positions most frequently mutated in major SARS-CoV-2 variants), moderate scores (0.05--0.3) to surrounding functional regions, and low noise (0.0--0.02) to background positions.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:440:Scores within each category are drawn from uniform distributions: $\mathcal{U}(0.8, 1.2)$ for seed positions, $\mathcal{U}(0.05, 0.3)$ for surrounding functional regions (defined as positions within 50 positions of each seed), and $\mathcal{U}(0.0, 0.02)$ for background. A single synthetic genome of 29,903 positions is generated per trial.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:441:Since the ground truth of synthetic data is known by design, this test evaluates each method's signal recovery capability but does not directly measure actual biological hotspot detection performance.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:442:Therefore, DMS-based validation (Section~\ref{subsec:dms_ground_truth}) and convergent evolution evaluation (Section~\ref{sec:multi_gt}) provide independent biological validation, confirming whether the conclusions from the synthetic benchmark hold on real data.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:501:Five variants were tested in Stage~1: the original implementation (v1, with a cumulative decay bug), the bug-fixed version (v2a), a dN/dS-filtered version (v2b), a CCM-seed + HDBSCAN hybrid (v2c), and a pure HDBSCAN baseline (v3).
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:505:MutClust-Hybrid (v2c) achieves its advantage through H-score-specific domain knowledge (CCM seed selection assumes H-score-like distributions), making it incompatible with non-H-score inputs such as ESM-2 LLR or pLDDT---its CCM seed logic becomes meaningless for these scoring types.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:600: & stability\_structural$^{\dagger}$ & Structure-weighted proxy & BLOSUM62 score weighted by ESMFold pLDDT (well-folded $\to$ higher impact) \\
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:622:\textbf{AI-based scores} leverage protein language models (PLMs) trained on large-scale protein sequence databases.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:625:The \texttt{stability} channel uses a BLOSUM62-based substitution proxy: at each MSA position, $\text{stability\_score} = -\overline{\text{BLOSUM62}(\text{wt}, \text{mut})}$ weighted by mutation frequency, so that radical substitutions (low BLOSUM62) yield higher destabilization scores. The \texttt{stability\_structural} variant multiplies this score by per-residue ESMFold pLDDT/100, reflecting that mutations in well-folded regions are more likely to disrupt structure. This proxy is used in place of full physics-based ($\Delta\Delta G$) predictors such as FoldX or RoseTTAFold, which are computationally infeasible at the 11-pathogen $\times$ 39-detector scale of MutBench.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:629:The \texttt{EVEscape\_composite} channel implements an EVEscape-style multiplicative combination~\cite{thadani2023evescape}: $\text{composite} = \text{ESM-2 LLR}_\text{norm} \times \text{SASA}_\text{norm} \times \text{Grantham}_\text{norm}$, where each component is min-max normalized to $[0, 1]$. This substitutes ESM-2 log-likelihood ratios for the original EVE fitness term, since EVE training is not feasible across all 11 pathogens within the present scope; the structural accessibility (SASA) and physicochemical dissimilarity (Grantham) terms follow the original EVEscape construction.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:651:SlidingTest & Sliding window statistical test & 2 \\
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:672:Supervised machine learning methods (e.g., Random Forest or gradient boosting classifiers) were not included because they require labeled training data at the position level, and with only 11 pathogens---each having 9--54 Layer~A positives---the available ground truth is insufficient for training generalizable classifiers without severe overfitting.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:676:For example, the Wavelet family is tested with three peak detection thresholds ($t = 1.0, 1.5, 2.0$ standard deviations above the CWT coefficient mean), and FreqThresh is tested with four percentile cutoffs (top 1\%, 3\%, 5\%, 10\%).
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:715:These methods select hotspots by applying a score cutoff: FreqThresh uses a fixed percentile threshold (top $k$\%), AdaptiveKnee automatically determines the threshold via knee-point detection on the sorted score curve, and AdaptWin extends seed positions above a percentile threshold bidirectionally to adjacent high-scoring positions.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:727:These methods apply statistical tests to identify positions or windows significantly deviating from the background: SlidingTest and SWAN use sliding-window $z$-tests against the global mean, LocalContrast computes local $z$-scores, GradPeak detects prominence-filtered peaks on smoothed profiles, and Bayes computes posterior hotspot probabilities from a prior and normalized scores.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:731:MutClust-Orig applies the original MutClust logic (CCM seed + adaptive DBSCAN) to MSA-based score profiles, serving as a reference baseline representing the prior state-of-the-art in domain-specific hotspot detection~\cite{youn2025mutclust}.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:732:Although MutClust uses DBSCAN clustering internally, it is separated from the Density/Clustering category because it constitutes a virus-specific pipeline (H-score computation $\to$ CCM seed selection $\to$ adaptive $\varepsilon$ clustering) rather than a generic density-based algorithm applied to arbitrary score profiles.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:766:These differences---unique sequence count (530--5,019), protein length (261--1,330 AA), temporal coverage ($\sim$2--50 years), and Layer~A positive rate (0.7--15.9\%)---reflect the real-world heterogeneity of available viral sequence data rather than a controlled experimental design. The ``pathogen'' factor in the ANOVA is therefore a composite variable that conflates biological differences with data availability differences.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:786:Layer B (constrained regions) is not included in MCC computation and is evaluated separately via constrained FPR. The majority of genomic positions belonging to neither Layer A nor B are classified as FP or TN depending on detection status.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:791:All enrichment tests used one-sided Fisher's exact test (alternative: greater), testing the directional hypothesis that hotspot positions are enriched for vaccine escape mutations relative to non-hotspot positions.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:792:\item \textbf{Constrained FPR}: The false positive rate in Layer B constrained regions.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:793:\item \textbf{DMS F1}: F1 score against Layer C DMS ground truth (computed only for 6 pathogens with DMS data).
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:818:Levene's test indicated heterogeneous variances across groups ($p < 0.05$); however, with $N = 8{,}580$ observations and a balanced design, ANOVA is robust to moderate violations of homoscedasticity.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:819:As a safeguard, all ANOVA findings were confirmed by the nonparametric Kruskal--Wallis test, which makes no distributional assumptions.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:820:Specifically, the Kruskal--Wallis test applied to the scoring main effect yielded $H = 277.9$, $p < 10^{-47}$, consistent with the parametric ANOVA result; this concordance confirms that the ANOVA conclusions are not artifacts of distributional assumptions. An additional Aligned Rank Transform (ART) two-way ANOVA on the scoring~$\times$~pathogen interaction (Wobbrock et al.\ 2011 procedure) yielded a rank-scale interaction $\omega^2 = 0.277$ with $F_{190, 2860} = 7.33$ and $p = 8.6 \times 10^{-141}$, distribution-free confirmation that the interaction is large and significant.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:821:No family-wise multiple testing correction (e.g., Bonferroni, Holm) was applied to the ANOVA results because the analysis is exploratory rather than confirmatory: the goal is to decompose variance sources, not to test individual pairwise comparisons. The Friedman test and LOPO cross-validation provide independent confirmation without requiring correction. For the vaccine escape Fisher's exact tests (3 comparisons), significance at $p < 0.01$ (H3N2, HIV-1) exceeds the Bonferroni-corrected threshold of $\alpha/3 = 0.017$.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:830:\subsubsection{LOPO Cross-Validation (Leave-One-Pathogen-Out)}
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:833:The best-performing combination is defined as the (scoring, family) pair with the highest mean MCC across the $n-1$ training pathogens.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:834:Through 11 iterations, the concordance rate between training-best and test-best (oracle) combinations and the performance gap are computed.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:839:A nonparametric repeated-measures test using 11 pathogens as blocks, the top $k = 20$ scoring $\times$ family combinations were compared to test whether statistically significant performance differences exist among them.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:877:\textit{Permutation test}: Two permutation approaches are employed.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:878:(1)~Random label shuffling: Through 1,000 random permutations of ground truth labels, it is tested whether the observed metrics significantly exceed random expectation.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:883:\textit{Pairwise comparison}: A paired bootstrap design that evaluates two methods simultaneously on the same bootstrap resample, testing the statistical significance of hotspot-score differences between methods.
chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:892:Per-pathogen feature AUC is computed via threshold sweeping (no model training), and a complementary multivariate Random Forest (\texttt{n\_estimators}~=~500, default scikit-learn hyperparameters, 5-fold cross-validation per pathogen) reports relative feature importances for triangulation.

chapters_en/ch3_methods.tex:898:The full source code, configuration files, scoring scripts, detection-family implementations, ground-truth tables, statistical-analysis notebooks, and the 8{,}580-evaluation result archive are released under an open-source license (see Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion}, Section~\ref{sec:code_availability} for the canonical repository URL, commit hash, and Zenodo DOI). The pinned random seed (\texttt{seed} = 42) governs all bootstrap, subsampling, and permutation analyses; library versions (Python~3.10, NumPy~1.24, SciPy~1.11, IQ-TREE~2, HyPhy~v2.5, ESM-2 \texttt{esm2\_t33\_650M\_UR50D}, FoldX~5) are pinned in the released environment file.

chapters_en/ch5_adapt.tex:25:\item \textbf{Structure-based} (2 features): \textit{plddt} (AlphaFold2/ESMFold predicted local distance difference test score~\cite{jumper2021alphafold}) and \textit{SASA} (relative solvent accessible surface area from ESMFold-predicted structures~\cite{shrake1973environment}).

chapters_en/ch5_adapt.tex:81:To assess feature importance in a multivariate context, a Random Forest classifier~\cite{breiman2001random} (200 trees, max depth 5, balanced class weights) was trained for each pathogen using the 10 features as predictors and Layer~A as the binary label.
chapters_en/ch5_adapt.tex:82:Feature importances were extracted as mean decrease in impurity (Gini importance), and model performance was evaluated via stratified 5-fold cross-validation AUC.
chapters_en/ch5_adapt.tex:101:To quantify each feature's contribution, three ablation analyses were conducted using the EqualWeight ensemble with LOPO evaluation and a top-10\% threshold (Figure~\ref{fig:feature_ablation_adapt}).

chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:21:Identifying hotspots in viral genomes is critical for three practical applications: (1)~predicting variant emergence by identifying positions predisposed to future mutations, (2)~selecting vaccine targets by avoiding highly mutable epitopes or targeting conserved adjacent regions, and (3)~developing broadly effective therapeutics that target structurally constrained positions unlikely to mutate without fitness cost.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:47:ConDor~\cite{morel2024condor} extends this approach to detect convergent amino acid substitutions across large protein alignments, using statistical tests to distinguish genuine convergence from chance recurrence.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:57:Rather than detecting spatial clusters of mutations, codon-based methods such as MEME (Mixed Effects Model of Evolution)~\cite{kosakovsky2020hyphy} and FUBAR (Fast Unconstrained Bayesian AppRoximation)~\cite{kosakovsky2020hyphy} estimate the ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous substitution rates ($\omega = dN/dS$) at each codon position.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:94:\textbf{Deep Mutational Scanning (DMS)} is an experimental technique that systematically measures the functional effects of all possible single amino acid substitutions within a protein~\cite{fowler2014dms}.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:95:In a typical DMS experiment, a library of mutant variants---each carrying a single amino acid substitution at one position---is generated through saturation mutagenesis.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:99:DMS is the gold standard for characterizing mutational effects because it is \textbf{unbiased} (every position and substitution is tested, not just those observed in nature), \textbf{comprehensive} (thousands of mutations are measured simultaneously in a single experiment), and \textbf{experimental} (fitness effects are directly measured rather than computationally predicted).
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:100:Unlike natural sequence variation, which reflects the combined effects of selection, drift, and sampling bias, DMS directly measures the intrinsic functional consequence of each mutation.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:102:Several landmark DMS studies have shaped our understanding of viral protein fitness landscapes.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:103:Starr et al.~\cite{starr2020dms} measured ACE2 binding affinity and protein expression for all single amino acid substitutions in the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD), revealing that most RBD positions are highly constrained for binding.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:105:Lee et al.~\cite{lee2018h3n2dms} performed DMS of influenza H3N2 hemagglutinin (HA), demonstrating that DMS fitness measurements can predict the evolutionary fates of naturally circulating variants.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:106:Bloom and Neher~\cite{bloom2023fitness} provided an integrated analysis of DMS fitness effects across all SARS-CoV-2 proteins, establishing a comprehensive reference for the entire viral proteome.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:108:Despite its power, DMS has important limitations.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:109:First, it is \textbf{expensive and labor-intensive}: each DMS experiment requires constructing a complete mutant library and performing selection assays, limiting its application to a small number of viral proteins.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:110:Second, most viral DMS studies use \textbf{pseudovirus systems} rather than authentic replication-competent virus, potentially missing fitness effects that depend on the complete viral replication cycle.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:111:Third, DMS measures fitness \textbf{in vitro}, which may not fully capture in vivo selective pressures such as immune evasion in the context of population-level immunity.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:112:Finally, DMS coverage across the viral world remains sparse: the EVEREST benchmark~\cite{gurev2025everest} catalogued only 45 DMS datasets across all WHO priority viruses, and comprehensive DMS data exist for fewer than 20 viral proteins.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:113:This availability gap means that DMS alone cannot serve as a universal ground truth for all pathogens---motivating MutBench's three-layer ground truth design (Chapter~\ref{ch:mutbench}), where DMS serves as Layer~C for the subset of pathogens with available data.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:115:DMS data provides a natural ground truth for hotspot benchmarking: positions where mutations exhibit large fitness effects correspond to biologically functional sites that detection methods should identify~\cite{livesey2020using}.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:116:Specifically, positions where the average DMS fitness effect of mutations is strongly negative (indicating functional constraint) or where specific mutations show large positive effects (indicating adaptive potential) are expected to overlap with biologically meaningful hotspots.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:117:Livesey and Marsh~\cite{livesey2020using} demonstrated that DMS datasets can serve as unbiased benchmarks for computational variant effect predictors, establishing a precedent for the use of DMS as ground truth in method evaluation.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:119:As a complementary approach, deep generative models have been shown to predict the effects of mutations from sequence variation alone~\cite{riesselman2018deep}, learning the statistical patterns of amino acid co-occurrence in evolutionarily related sequences to infer functional constraints without experimental data.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:120:This approach was extended by EVE~\cite{frazer2021eve}, a Bayesian variational autoencoder (VAE) that learns evolutionary constraints from multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) without requiring experimental labels.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:122:The success of EVE and related generative models suggests that evolutionary information encoded in natural sequence variation captures much of the same functional signal as DMS experiments, albeit with lower resolution for individual mutations.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:128:Protein language models (PLMs) trained on large-scale protein sequence databases have emerged as a complementary computational approach to variant effect prediction.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:129:The fundamental insight underlying PLMs is that evolutionary constraints on protein function are implicitly encoded in the patterns of amino acid co-occurrence across millions of naturally evolved sequences.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:130:By training transformer-based architectures on these patterns, PLMs learn a representation of ``evolutionary plausibility'' that can be used to score mutations without requiring structural data or experimental fitness measurements.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:132:\textbf{ESM-2}~\cite{lin2023esm2,rives2021biological} is a masked language model with 650 million parameters, trained on approximately 250 million protein sequences from the UniRef database.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:134:Negative LLR values indicate that the mutation is disfavored relative to the wild-type, suggesting functional constraint, while positive values suggest the mutation may be tolerated or even beneficial.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:136:A critical consideration is that ESM-2 was trained predominantly on cellular organism proteins from UniRef; viral proteins, which constitute a small fraction of the training data and exhibit evolutionary dynamics distinct from eukaryotic and prokaryotic proteins, may not be equally well represented in the learned embedding space.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:139:Unlike ESM-2's masked (bidirectional) architecture, Tranception's autoregressive design captures directional dependencies and can incorporate retrieval-augmented inference using homologous sequences at test time.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:142:\textbf{ProtTrans}~\cite{elnaggar2022prottrans} adopts transformer architectures (including BERT and T5 variants) pretrained on UniRef and BFD databases totaling over 2 billion protein sequences, achieving competitive performance on protein function prediction tasks including secondary structure prediction and localization.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:147:EVEscape integrates three components to predict viral immune escape mutations: (1)~EVE fitness scores from a Bayesian variational autoencoder trained on MSAs, (2)~structural accessibility from experimentally determined structures (PDB) or AlphaFold predictions, and (3)~physicochemical dissimilarity between wildtype and mutant residues (charge and hydrophobicity changes).
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:151:However, its training data and evaluation are centered on human genetic variants, and the distinct evolutionary dynamics of viral proteins---rapid evolution, high mutation rates, and population-level rather than individual-level selection---limit the direct applicability of AlphaMissense to viral variant effect prediction.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:159:The most comprehensive benchmark for PLM-based variant effect prediction is ProteinGym~\cite{notin2023proteingym}, which evaluates over 70 predictors on 217 DMS assays spanning 2.7 million substitution variants, primarily from human and model organism proteins.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:160:ProteinGym has been instrumental in establishing performance rankings among PLMs and alignment-based methods for the per-mutation fitness prediction task: given a specific amino acid substitution at a specific position, predict its continuous fitness effect (evaluated by Spearman correlation against DMS measurements).
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:172:\textbf{Nextstrain}~\cite{nextstrain2018hadfield} integrates phylogenetic analysis with geographic and temporal metadata to track pathogen evolution in real time. Its primary function is to answer ``which lineages are currently spreading and where?''---for example, tracking the geographic expansion of SARS-CoV-2 Omicron sublineages or seasonal influenza clades. Nextstrain visualizes the evolutionary relationships among circulating variants but does not evaluate or compare methods for detecting mutation-prone positions.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:183:Other surveillance-related resources include \textbf{GISAID}~\cite{shu2017gisaid}, the primary repository for pathogen genome sequences providing the raw data from which mutation frequencies are computed, and \textbf{outbreak.info}, which aggregates variant prevalence data from GISAID.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:198:This result highlights that mutual information between positions---capturing the constraint network within protein structures---provides predictive power beyond what single-position features can offer. The broader DCA / EVcouplings / GREMLIN family of position-coupling methods is intentionally outside the 20-scoring panel of MutBench (Section~\ref{sec:scoring_detection}), which restricts itself to single-position scorers to enable the orthogonal scoring~$\times$~detection-family ANOVA decomposition; epistasis-aware extensions are flagged as future work in Chapter~\ref{ch:discussion}.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:236:(1)~ProteinGym~\cite{notin2023proteingym,notin2025proteingym_v13}, which benchmarks variant effect predictors using 217 DMS assays and 90+ baseline models (as of v1.3) but addresses a per-residue fitness-regression task rather than hotspot region detection;
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:237:(1b)~\textbf{ViroGym}~\cite{virogym2026} (Mar 2026), which benchmarks PLM and alignment-based scorers across 13 viruses, 79 DMS assays, 552{,}937 sequences, and 7 phenotypic categories including immune escape---larger virus count than MutBench, but focused on per-variant fitness rather than per-region detection;
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:246:Recent years have seen significant progress in benchmarking variant effect prediction (VEP) methods on proteins. ProteinGym~\cite{notin2023proteingym} established a large-scale benchmark comprising 217 DMS assays and 2.7 million substitution variants, primarily for human and model organism proteins. EVE~\cite{frazer2021eve}, a Bayesian VAE trained on evolutionary sequences, demonstrated that unsupervised generative models can predict disease-associated variants without clinical labels. EVEscape~\cite{thadani2023evescape} extended this framework to viral immune escape prediction by combining EVE fitness scores with structural accessibility and physicochemical dissimilarity, successfully forecasting SARS-CoV-2 Omicron escape mutations from pre-pandemic data.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:248:Most recently, EVEREST~\cite{gurev2025everest,gurev2026everest_v3} specifically benchmarked VEP methods across WHO priority viruses; the v3 expansion (Jan 2026) covers 45 viral DMS datasets, 31 forecasting clades across 4 viruses, and reliability assessment across 40 WHO priority RNA viruses spanning 16 viral families. EVEREST finds that protein language models substantially underperform alignment-based approaches on viral proteins, that reliability fails for over half of the WHO-40 panel (especially surface glycoproteins), and that prediction reliability varies dramatically across pathogens---a finding that independently corroborates the LOPO 0/11 non-transferability reported in MutBench Chapter~\ref{ch:results}.
chapters_en/ch2_background.tex:249:The PLANT framework~\cite{plant2025antigenic} and Shah et al.~\cite{shah2024h3n2ml} provide PLM-based and ML-based H3N2 antigenic cartography that explicitly competes with WHO vaccine-strain selection, building on the foundational antigenic-cartography paradigm of Smith et al.~\cite{smith2004antigenic}; MutBench's H3N2 self-consistency check (Section~\ref{sec:cross_validation_escape}) is positioned as a detection-side complement to these prediction-side cartographies, not as a competitor.
