chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:24:The real GISAID benchmark (Section~\ref{sec:real_gisaid_benchmark}) demonstrated that the sparse distribution of real H-scores (342/29,903 nonzero) fundamentally changes detection dynamics: MutClust-Hybrid's synthetic advantage disappears (hotspot-score 0.383 vs.\ 0.386 for MutClust-Fixed).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:25:However, enrichment ratios remain 6.9--8.0-fold above random, confirming that biological signal is preserved despite the F1 drop.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:32:The synthetic benchmark's ground truth is defined independently of the detection methods (DMS experimental data and convergent evolution literature), ensuring no \emph{algorithmic} circularity between evaluation and detection.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:35:To provide a frequency-independent validation dimension, Layer~C (DMS experimental fitness) is used where available (6 of 11 pathogens), and the vaccine escape enrichment analysis (Section~\ref{sec:vaccine_escape}) provides partial external cross-validation: HIV-1 (82\% of its escape set disjoint from Layer~A) is the cleanest external anchor, whereas H3N2's 69\% Layer~A/escape overlap means that the H3N2 enrichment re-measures benchmark performance more than it provides independent replication. The circularity audit in Chapter~\ref{ch:results} Table~\ref{tab:vaccine_escape_stage3} reports novel-only enrichment values that quantify this distinction.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:36:The biological validity of detected hotspots was further supported by 3D structural analysis (Section~\ref{sec:structure_analysis}), which showed 5.92-fold spatial contact enrichment, and by the consistent superiority of domain-specific methods (MutClust variants) over general-purpose alternatives (OPTICS, KDE) in Section~\ref{sec:external_comparison}.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:48:TC-freq achieved the highest enrichment ratio (3.43-fold) on convergent evolution ground truth, suggesting that temporal contrast scoring is a viable direction; the appropriate temporal resolution remains a future challenge.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:55:In the multiple ground truth evaluation (Section~\ref{sec:multi_gt}), the Jaccard similarity between DMS-escape and convergent evolution positions was only 0.006, confirming that the two measures capture fundamentally different aspects of variation.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:57:The result that the best method varies depending on the ground truth suggests that the ``best hotspot detection method'' is context-dependent: for immune evasion studies, methods best suited for the convergent evolution criterion are preferred, while for molecular function studies, methods best suited for the DMS criterion are preferred.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:79:The cross-pathogen benchmark demonstrated that no universally best-performing method exists (Chapter~\ref{ch:results}), with implications for real-time surveillance systems such as Nextstrain~\cite{nextstrain2018hadfield}: applying a previously optimized combination to a new pathogen may not generalize.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:80:The underlying cause is that pathogen-specific genomic characteristics create fundamentally different signal landscapes---for example, H3N2's uniformly nonzero H-scores neutralize threshold-based seed detection, while MERS's sparse genome favors weak-signal detectors.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:92:\textbf{EVEREST}~\cite{gurev2025everest} benchmarked variant effect prediction (VEP) methods across 45 viral DMS datasets and found that protein language models substantially underperform alignment-based approaches on viral proteins, with prediction reliability varying dramatically across pathogens. This parallels MutBench's finding that the optimal \textit{information source} is pathogen-dependent, with the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction as the largest variance component. However, EVEREST evaluates per-mutation fitness prediction (continuous Spearman correlation), whereas MutBench evaluates per-region hotspot detection (binary MCC classification). The convergence of both studies on the pathogen-dependence conclusion---despite addressing fundamentally different problems---strengthens the generality of this finding.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:100:\textbf{ProteinGym}~\cite{notin2023proteingym} showed that VEP model performance varies across the 217 DMS assays in its benchmark. While ProteinGym focuses on human and model organism proteins, MutBench demonstrates the same pattern in viral proteins, with the additional finding that the choice of \textit{input information type}---not just the computational model---is the dominant performance factor.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:102:In summary, the pathogen-dependence of optimal methods is not unique to MutBench but appears to be a general principle across variant effect prediction (EVEREST, ProteinGym), feature analysis (Maher et al.), escape prediction (Hie et al.), and driver detection (Bailey et al.). MutBench's contribution is to quantify this dependence through variance decomposition ($\omega^2 = 0.296$ at 20-type granularity; 0.103 at 6-category granularity as a collinearity-robust lower bound) and to illustrate practical consequence through vaccine-escape cross-validation, with HIV-1 (7.19-fold enrichment, 82\% disjoint from Layer~A) as the primary external anchor and H3N2 (9.36-fold) as a self-consistency check given 69\% Layer~A/escape overlap.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:155:Second, \textit{multi-source integration recovers positions missed by single-information approaches}. For H3N2, frequency-based scoring misses antigenic site~B positions (155, 159, 160) that are structurally constrained, but the EqualWeight ensemble captures them through the pLDDT and homoplasy components (Section~\ref{subsec:search_space_reduction}). This complementarity---where different information types detect different subsets of positions---is the mechanistic basis for the dominant scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:159:The primary risk of missed positions lies in pathogens with low recall: EV-A71 (recall = 0.185) and Rabies (recall = 0.308). For these pathogens, the 261~AA and 491~AA post-truncation alignment lengths provide limited statistical power, and the small number of detected positions ($n = 10$ and $n = 39$, respectively) may not adequately represent the full landscape of adaptive sites. Users applying MutBench to such short-protein pathogens should interpret the detected positions as a prioritized subset rather than an exhaustive list, and complement computational detection with experimental validation (DMS or epitope mapping).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:164:Returning to the three problems identified in Chapter~\ref{ch:introduction}: the standardised evaluation framework is provided by the three-layer ground truth and hotspot-score metric (Contribution~1); pathogen-dependence is quantified by the interaction effect ($\omega^2 = 0.296$) and corroborated by LOPO 0/11 (Contribution~2); cross-validation against vaccine-escape positions establishes practical relevance, anchored by HIV-1 (Contribution~3).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:173:While LOPO cross-validation yields 0/11 generalization, MutBench provides practical value through three mechanisms: (1)~the family-level scoring recommendation table (Table~\ref{tab:scoring_recommendation} in this chapter) provides coarse-grained guidance based on virus family characteristics; (2)~the 4-feature EqualWeight ensemble achieves 4.012-fold vaccine escape enrichment without requiring pathogen-specific optimization; and (3)~for any new pathogen with $\geq$200 sequences, the full 8,580-evaluation benchmark completes in approximately 25~seconds on a single workstation, making exhaustive evaluation operationally feasible.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:199:\paragraph{Three-tier evidence rule.} Pathogens are assigned to one of three evidence tiers using two operational criteria evaluated jointly: (i)~\emph{Bonferroni survival} of the Fisher's exact $p$-value across 780 scoring--detection combinations ($p_{\text{adj}} < 0.05$), and (ii)~\emph{Layer~A independence}, defined as fewer than one-third of escape positions overlapping the pathogen's Layer~A set ($|\text{escape} \cap \text{Layer A}| / |\text{escape}| < 33\%$). A pathogen passing both criteria is classified as a \textbf{primary external anchor} (HIV-1: 18\% overlap, $p_{\text{adj}} = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$); a pathogen passing only (i)~is a \textbf{self-consistency check} (H3N2: 69\% overlap, $p_{\text{adj}} = 2.6 \times 10^{-5}$); a pathogen passing neither is reported as \textbf{exploratory} (SARS-CoV-2: $p_{\text{adj}} > 0.05$). The 33\% overlap threshold separates the three observed pathogens into distinct tiers without intermediate values; sensitivity to the threshold (25\%, 33\%, 50\%) does not change tier assignments for these three cases. With only three pathogens any threshold in $(18\%, 60\%)$ produces the same partition; the rule is therefore calibrated on observed data and explicitly underpowered as a *predictive* rule for new pathogens. Future cycles with additional escape-annotated pathogens will test whether the 33\% threshold remains the correct cut-point; the present work uses it as a transparent decision rule, not a generalised threshold.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:201:HIV-1 is the cleanest external validation: its escape set shares only 8 of 45 positions (18\%) with HIV-1 Layer~A, so the 7.19$\times$ enrichment (Bonferroni-adjusted $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$) primarily reflects detection of positions outside the benchmark's training signal. A direct novel-only re-test on the 37 Layer~A-disjoint positions (best combination freq~$+$~Wavelet~$t = 1.5$) yields enrichment in the range $7.16\text{--}8.24\times$ depending on how many of the 8 escape~$\cap$~Layer-A positions the detector also captures (sensitivity $k \in \{0, \ldots, 8\}$); even the conservative worst case ($k = 8$, all overlap positions detected) gives $7.16\times$ with Fisher $p = 5.0 \times 10^{-12}$, which survives Bonferroni correction ($\times 780$) by more than nine orders of magnitude.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:207:\textbf{Concurrent-benchmark task-orthogonality.} The MutBench panel overlaps with ViroGym (HIV, SARS-CoV-2, H3N2 are common) and EVEREST~v3 (HIV, SARS-CoV-2 forecasting clades), so a head-to-head leaderboard appears feasible in principle. We do not run one in this dissertation because the metric universes are structurally non-overlapping: ViroGym and EVEREST optimise per-variant fitness Spearman against DMS, while MutBench optimises per-region binary MCC against the 3-layer ground truth; converting between the two requires either (a) thresholding fitness predictions at a top-$k$ cutoff to obtain a binary region call (which throws away the continuous information ViroGym/EVEREST were optimised for), or (b) summarising MutBench detections into a fitness ranking (which throws away the spatial-clustering information MutBench was optimised for). Either reduction biases the comparison toward the receiving format. The principled task-aligned subset evaluation (binarise fitness predictions at top-$k$ thresholds matched to MutBench's positive-rate per pathogen, then compare MCC on the shared HIV/SARS-CoV-2/H3N2 panel) is queued as a defense-week sprint item (Chapter~\ref{ch:conclusion} Table~\ref{tab:limitations_summary}); the present cycle's contribution is the *structural orthogonality argument* itself, which removes the head-to-head as a knock-down objection.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:209:This cross-validation is particularly important for the five pathogens without DMS data (Layer~C), where benchmark validity rests primarily on Layer~A.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:210:The EVEREST study and its v3 expansion~\cite{gurev2025everest,gurev2026everest_v3} demonstrate that even with 45 DMS datasets, current models fail to reliably predict mutations in over half of the 40 WHO priority RNA viruses, with reliability worst for surface glycoproteins---an external finding that independently corroborates the LOPO 0/11 non-transferability reported in Chapter~\ref{ch:results}. For H3N2 specifically, the antigenic-cartography lineage of Smith et al.~\cite{smith2004antigenic} and the recent PLM-based extensions of PLANT~\cite{plant2025antigenic} and Shah et al.~\cite{shah2024h3n2ml} target a prediction task complementary to MutBench's region-level detection; the 69\% Layer~A overlap reported above should therefore be interpreted as task-internal self-consistency rather than as a head-to-head antigenic-prediction claim.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:211:MutBench's combination of Layer~A benchmark rankings with independent vaccine escape validation provides complementary evidence that circumvents DMS data availability constraints, supporting the validity of Layer~A as a ground truth even for pathogens where DMS data are unavailable.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:219:For public health practitioners, MutBench results can be operationalized through the following workflow when a novel pathogen or variant emerges: (1)~compute the 20 scoring types from the available MSA (requiring only sequence data and publicly available tools: MAFFT for alignment, HyPhy for FUBAR, ESM-2 for PLM scores, AlphaFold2 for structural features); (2)~if the pathogen belongs to a family already represented in MutBench (e.g., Coronaviridae, Orthomyxoviridae, Flaviviridae), use the family-level scoring recommendation from Table~\ref{tab:scoring_recommendation} as a starting point; (3)~if the pathogen is novel, apply the EqualWeight ensemble as a conservative baseline, which achieves 98\% of full-feature performance with only 4 core features (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency). This workflow integrates with existing surveillance platforms such as Nextstrain~\cite{nextstrain2018hadfield} and GISAID~\cite{shu2017gisaid}, which already provide the MSA inputs required by MutBench.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:228:Retrieve $\geq$200 protein-coding sequences from NCBI GenBank or GISAID, ensuring temporal and geographic diversity. Construct a multiple sequence alignment using MAFFT~\cite{katoh2013mafft} (${\sim}$5 minutes for 1{,}000 sequences).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:231:Compute scoring features in order of increasing computational cost: (i)~frequency and Shannon entropy from the MSA (seconds); (ii)~homoplasy counts via Fitch parsimony on an inferred phylogenetic tree (2--5 minutes); (iii)~ESM-2 log-likelihood ratios, requiring a GPU (3--5 minutes per protein); (iv)~structural features such as surface accessibility and interface proximity, requiring an AlphaFold2~\cite{jumper2021alphafold} predicted structure or an experimental PDB entry when available. Steps (i)--(iii) are applicable to any pathogen with $\geq$200 sequences and require no specialized hardware beyond a single GPU for ESM-2 inference; step (iv) can be omitted when no structural model exists, with moderate impact on detection performance. When structural features are available, the 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) captures 98\% of full-ensemble performance; without pLDDT, the remaining 3 features (homoplasy, entropy, frequency) still provide the dominant scoring signals.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:256:Apply KDE or Wavelet-based detection as robust defaults (Section~\ref{sec:external_comparison}). If ground truth positions are available (e.g., from DMS experiments or literature), compute the hotspot-score metric. When scoring features are pre-computed, detection and evaluation across all 39 detector configurations completes in under 3~seconds per pathogen (the full 8,580-evaluation benchmark requires approximately 25~seconds).
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:259:The total pipeline runtime per pathogen is approximately 15--20 minutes on a workstation equipped with a single GPU (tested on NVIDIA RTX 3090). The most time-consuming step is ESM-2 inference; all other steps complete in under 10 minutes on a standard CPU. No specialized high-performance computing infrastructure is required.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:260:For resource-constrained settings, the 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) achieves statistically indistinguishable performance from the full 10-feature ensemble (MCC 0.081 vs.\ 0.083) while requiring only MSA-based computation and a single AlphaFold2 query---eliminating the need for GPU-intensive ESM-2 inference and reducing runtime to under 10 minutes per pathogen.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:270:Validation on real GISAID sequences (Section~\ref{subsec:treetime_gisaid_validation}) showed that H-score and homoplasy score capture fundamentally different signals ($\rho = -0.107$, $p = 1.36 \times 10^{-4}$), supporting the practical value of homoplasy-based correction.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:275:\subsection{Representativeness and Sampling Bias of GISAID Data}
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:277:Systematic biases exist in the GISAID~\cite{shu2017gisaid}-based input data.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:283:Temporal analysis on SARS-CoV-2 Spike across three 6-month windows reveals that feature discriminative power changes substantially: frequency AUC increases from 0.337 (2020-H1) to 0.472 (2021-H1), and entropy AUC from 0.328 to 0.507, as mean Shannon entropy rises 10-fold (0.126 to 1.241) with accumulating diversity.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:289:ESM-2~\cite{lin2023esm2} was trained on UniRef50/UniRef90, which contains viral protein sequences, and the 11 target proteins in our benchmark (e.g., SARS-CoV-2 Spike, HIV-1 gp120, H3N2 HA) are likely present in the training corpus.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:292:The semantic change feature (cosine distance between wild-type and mutant embeddings) is less susceptible to this concern because it measures relative embedding shifts rather than absolute likelihoods, making it more robust to training set memorization.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:293:Future work should evaluate protein language models trained on databases that exclude viral sequences to quantify the magnitude of this potential bias. \textbf{Concurrent-benchmark reconciliation}: EVEREST v3 reports that PLMs underperform alignment-based methods on viral DMS \emph{fitness regression}, while the present work finds PLMs winning on 2 of 11 pathogens for region-level \emph{detection} (RSV best ESM-2 LLR; SARS-CoV-2 best Tranception). The two findings are compatible because the tasks differ structurally (per-variant continuous Spearman vs.\ per-region binary MCC), and the fact that Norovirus's best is homoplasy (AUC 0.944) rather than a PLM is exactly the pattern leakage-driven inflation would not predict.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:299:A methodological limitation concerns the \emph{winner's curse}~\cite{ioannidis2008winner}: with 780 candidate combinations searched per pathogen and the highest-MCC combination retained, the reported top-1 enrichment is an upper-envelope estimate rather than a typical value (the Bonferroni-survivor mean enrichment is materially lower; H3N2 mean $\approx 4.7\times$ vs.\ top $9.36\times$). The winner's-curse formulation is one face of the broader question of multiple testing correction when selecting the best scoring--detection combination per pathogen. At the detection-family level (20 scoring $\times$ 14 families = 280 combinations evaluated per pathogen), the probability that 11 out of 11 pathogens exhibit unique best combinations by chance alone is approximately 82\% under uniform random assignment ($\prod_{i=0}^{10} (280-i)/280 \approx 0.820$); at the parameter-variant level (20 scoring $\times$ 39 variants = 780 combinations, as reported in Section~\ref{subsec:9pathogen_statistical}), the same probability is approximately 93\%. The choice of aggregation level matters: the family-level calculation is the more conservative reference for cross-pathogen uniqueness because parameter-variant collapsing to families reduces the effective combinatorial space. However, several factors mitigate this concern: (1)~the best combinations are not merely unique but involve 9~distinct scoring \textit{types} from 4~of~6 categories, which has much lower random probability; (2)~the ANOVA interaction effect ($\omega^2 = 0.296$) quantifies systematic rather than chance variation; and (3)~the vaccine escape enrichment cross-validation confirms that benchmark-optimal methods also achieve the highest enrichment on independently curated escape positions. Nevertheless, future work should apply permutation-based significance testing to determine whether each pathogen's best combination is statistically distinguishable from alternatives.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:303:\textbf{Independent reproduction.} The 8{,}580-evaluation benchmark was produced by a single team using a single codebase against a single GISAID snapshot, with random seed~$=42$ and fully scripted configuration (Section~\ref{sec:code_availability}). Independent multi-tool reproduction on the same pathogen panel is queued for the next cycle (Priority~5)---a gap analogous to that identified by Bailey et al.~\cite{bailey2018comprehensive} prior to the PanCancer reproducibility effort.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:311:The 20 scoring types do not operate under identical conditions. Frequency and entropy scores require only the MSA, making them the most standardized. Phylogenetic scores (FUBAR, dN/dS, homoplasy) additionally depend on phylogenetic tree quality, which varies across pathogens: H3N2's well-sampled multi-decade tree provides more reliable dN/dS estimates than MERS's sparse 5-year phylogeny. Structure-based scores (pLDDT, SASA) depend on predicted structure accuracy, which is higher for well-characterized proteins (SARS-CoV-2 Spike) than for less-studied ones (EV-A71 VP1). AI-based scores inherit biases from their training data, as discussed above.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:312:This input heterogeneity means that a scoring type's performance reflects not only the informativeness of its underlying biological signal but also the quality of auxiliary inputs (trees, structures, training data) available for each pathogen. The scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction therefore captures both genuine biological signal differences and input quality differences, which cannot be fully separated without controlled experiments using standardized auxiliary inputs.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:328:Additionally, HCV has an effective Layer~B size of 0 (constrained regions could not be mapped within the alignment length), meaning HCV evaluation relies solely on Layer~A. This asymmetry should be considered when interpreting HCV-specific results.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:329:Future work could address this by incorporating structurally constrained positions from experimental HCV E2 structures or conservation analysis across Hepacivirus species.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:335:Despite the small sample size ($n=11$), the Friedman test yielded $p=0.990$, indicating that no single method can be reliably distinguished as superior across all pathogens. This is consistent with the LOPO finding (0/11 match rate) that each pathogen requires a unique best-performing combination. \textbf{Sampling-quality vs.\ pathogen-dependence}: the smallest-sample pathogens (Rabies $n_{\text{seq}} = 2{,}038$ but truncated 491 AA; EV-A71 $n_{\text{seq}} = 662$, 261 AA) do attain the lowest oracle MCCs (0.248, 0.260), so a sampling-quality confound is not zero. However, the technical-covariate sensitivity analysis (Section~\ref{sec:scoring_input_heterogeneity}, $\rho_L = -0.73$, $\rho_P = +0.64$) shows the joint covariate effect is subsumed by the pathogen main effect ($\omega^2 = 0.117$), and the scoring~$\times$~pathogen interaction (0.296) is a within-pathogen quantity that survives this absorption (see the ANCOVA bound there). Excluding the two smallest-sample pathogens (re-running the ANOVA on $n = 9$) shifts the headline interaction by less than the cluster-bootstrap CI half-width, so the pathogen-dependence finding is not a small-sample artifact of the two weakest panels.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:337:The LOPO result should be interpreted with caution given the small sample size ($n = 11$). With only 10 training pathogens per fold, the power to detect a generalizable best combination is inherently limited. The 0/11 match rate is consistent with two interpretations: (1)~truly pathogen-specific optimality with no cross-pathogen generalization, or (2)~insufficient sample size to identify a robust generalizable pattern. The large mean performance gap (0.265 MCC) between oracle and generalized predictions supports interpretation~(1), but a definitive distinction requires a larger pathogen panel.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:344:The AI-based scoring types (ESM-2 LLR, Tranception, semantic change, stability predictors) were evaluated using pre-trained models without virus-specific fine-tuning. The performance of these models is constrained by the composition of their training data: ESM-2 was trained on UniRef50 (general proteins), which includes limited representation of rapidly evolving viral surface proteins. Fine-tuning on viral protein families or using virus-specific language models could potentially improve performance but was not evaluated in this study. Recent work on CoVFit~\cite{covfit2025}, which fine-tunes ESM-2 on SARS-CoV-2 epidemiological and DMS data, demonstrates that pathogen-specific adaptation of PLMs can substantially improve fitness prediction---consistent with MutBench's central finding that the optimal information source is pathogen-dependent. Additionally, the comparison between sequence-based (ESM-2) and structure-conditioned (stability\_structural) predictors does not control for the quality of input structures, which varies across pathogens depending on the availability of experimentally determined structures versus AlphaFold2 predictions.
chapters_en/ch5_discussion.tex:347:The MSA sequences used in this benchmark were downloaded from NCBI GenBank without controlling for geographic or temporal sampling bias. Surveillance intensity varies dramatically across pathogens and regions: SARS-CoV-2 sequences are dominated by high-income country submissions during 2020--2022, while Rabies and EV-A71 sequences reflect more geographically diverse but temporally sparse sampling. This sampling heterogeneity may inflate mutation frequencies at founder-effect positions in over-sampled lineages (e.g., SARS-CoV-2 D614G) while underrepresenting diversity in under-sampled regions. The Layer~A ground truth partially mitigates this concern by requiring independent emergence across multiple lineages, but Layer~A position counts themselves may be biased toward well-studied pathogens.

chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:25:As a controlled signal recovery test, synthetic H-scores were generated for a SARS-CoV-2-like genome (29,903 positions) with 1,251 ground truth functional positions.

chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:52:However, on actual GISAID data (Section~\ref{sec:real_gisaid_benchmark}) F1 drops to 0.123 due to sparse H-score distributions, so this synthetic benchmark validates discriminative ability under controlled conditions only.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:59:Detection methods were therefore evaluated against three complementary ground truths: \textbf{functional regions} (439 AA, 34.5\% of Spike; domain annotations including RBD, NTD supersite, furin cleavage, fusion peptide, HR1, HR2), \textbf{DMS-escape} (252 positions, 19.8\%; top 20th percentile of experimentally measured fitness effects~\cite{dadonaite2023dms}), and \textbf{convergent evolution} (97 positions, 7.6\%; literature-based recurrent positive selection sites~\cite{cao2023ba286,carabelli2023convergent}).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:60:The three are largely non-overlapping (Jaccard similarity between DMS-escape and convergent evolution = 0.006), confirming that they capture fundamentally different aspects of mutational importance.

chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:119:To address circularity concerns with synthetic data, a benchmark was conducted using actual GISAID 2020--2021 H-score data~\cite{youn2025mutclust}.

chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:164:\textbf{Stage 1 summary.} MutClust-Hybrid achieves the best hotspot-score (0.778) on synthetic data, but all methods show reduced performance on real GISAID data (F1: 0.785 $\to$ 0.123) due to sparse H-score distributions, while maintaining biological validity (enrichment $>$ 6.9-fold).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:174:All detection results are statistically significant: permutation tests (1,000 random and 200 circular iterations) yielded $p < 0.005$ for all methods ($z > 9.2$).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:209:Enrichment ratios also decreased (0.87--2.36-fold vs.\ 1.9--23.7-fold for SARS-CoV-2), reflecting the short HA gene and high background mutation rate.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:210:Figure~\ref{fig:cross_pathogen_comparison} directly compares the top-5 scoring-type MCC across all 11 pathogens in Stage~2, illustrating that the optimal scoring type shifts substantially from pathogen to pathogen (e.g., FUBAR pos.\ for SARS-CoV-2, FUBAR Bayes factor for H3N2, homoplasy for Norovirus, EqualWeight for HIV-1 and MERS, pLDDT-inv for RSV, dN/dS for Influenza~B and HCV, stability-based scores for Rabies and EV-A71). This heterogeneity provides direct visual evidence that no universal best method exists across the 11-pathogen panel, complementing the ANOVA interaction effect (Section~\ref{subsec:9pathogen_statistical}) and the LOPO 0/11 match rate (Section~\ref{subsec:9pathogen_lopo}).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:219:3D structural analysis using C$\alpha$ coordinates from PDB 6VSB confirmed that linear-sequence hotspots are also spatially clustered, with a \textbf{5.92-fold spatial contact enrichment} over random pairs ($z$ = 13.34, 1,000 permutations).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:249:This section sequentially reports the benchmark scale, per-pathogen best method analysis, analysis of variance, cross-validation, and statistical test results.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:259:Each evaluation computed MCC, F1, precision, and recall against the 3-layer ground truth (Layer A: convergent evolution positions, Layer B: constrained regions, Layer C: DMS).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:260:DMS Layer~C evaluation was conducted for 6 pathogens (SARS-CoV-2, H3N2, HIV-1, RSV, Rabies, EV-A71) where experimental fitness data are available.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:261:All FASTA sequences were collected from NCBI GenBank using actual accession numbers.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:301:The more substantive finding is not the uniqueness itself but the large performance gap between oracle and generalized selection (mean MCC gap $= 0.265$ from LOPO cross-validation), which demonstrates that the \emph{correct} choice of combination matters significantly even though many combinations exist.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:303:While the finding that different pathogens favor different methods might appear self-evident, the non-trivial contribution lies in three aspects: (1)~quantifying the magnitude of this interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$, explaining 29.6\% of variance---far exceeding the scoring main effect of 6.3\%); (2)~demonstrating that the information \textit{type} (not the detection algorithm) is the dominant factor; and (3)~showing that even with only 11~pathogens, no cross-pathogen generalization is achievable (LOPO 0/11), establishing that pathogen-adaptive selection is necessary rather than merely beneficial.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:318:\item \textbf{SARS-CoV-2 --- Tranception}: With a shallow pandemic phylogeny (originating $\sim$2019), frequency-based signals are dominated by founder effects. Protein language models capture broader evolutionary constraints learned from diverse coronavirus families, compensating for limited within-species phylogenetic depth---a finding independently corroborated by the SARS-CoV-2--specific CoVFit PLM~\cite{covfit2025}, which fine-tunes ESM-2 on surveillance and DMS data and reports analogous PLM-driven gains over frequency-only baselines.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:319:\item \textbf{RSV --- ESM-2 LLR}: RSV F protein is under antibody-mediated selection, but the limited phylogenetic diversity of sequenced RSV strains weakens frequency and phylogenetic signals. ESM-2's learned evolutionary constraints provide an alternative information source.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:320:\item \textbf{Rabies --- stability}: Rabies G protein mediates cell entry through a pH-triggered conformational change, making structural stability a key functional constraint. Positions where stability-altering mutations are tolerated indicate adaptive flexibility.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:394:The same 8{,}580-evaluation dataset is re-examined under three statistical lenses: ANOVA (interaction $\omega^2 = 0.296$, CI [0.195, 0.333]); Friedman ($\chi^2 = 7.69$, $p = 0.990$); LOPO (0/11 matches, gap 0.265). The three lenses are consistency checks on the same data, not independent replications; an independent replication on a disjoint pathogen panel is deferred to future work.

chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:400:LOPO (Leave-One-Pathogen-Out) cross-validation was performed to evaluate whether the best combination selected from 10 training pathogens generalizes to the excluded test pathogen (Figure~\ref{fig:lopo_crossval}).

chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:427:These results are consistent with a key interpretation: the 0/11 exact-match rate is itself not unexpected given 780 unique scoring--detection combinations (Section~\ref{subsec:9pathogen_statistical}), so the primary evidence for pathogen-adaptive method selection is not the exact-match rate but the accompanying mean oracle-vs-generalized MCC gap of 0.265 (family-level oracle mean 0.297; generalized mean 0.032), which quantifies the performance cost of ignoring pathogen identity.\footnote{All LOPO arithmetic in this section uses the scoring~$\times$~detection-family aggregation (280 combinations); the larger detector-variant oracle of 0.341 reported in the per-combination headline (Section~\ref{subsec:9pathogen_bootstrap}) corresponds to the finer scoring~$\times$~detector-variant grid (780 combinations) and is not directly comparable to the 0.265 gap.}
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:431:Using the 11 pathogens as blocks, a Friedman test was performed on the performance differences among the top 20 scoring--detection family combinations.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:440:The LOPO performance gap of 0.265 MCC (family-level oracle mean 0.297 vs.\ generalized mean 0.032) and the per-pathogen oracle MCC range (0.196--0.660) support interpretation~(2): methods perform well on their respective pathogens but fail to generalize, producing inconsistent cross-pathogen rankings rather than uniformly low performance.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:443:At the detection-family level (280 scoring--family combinations; matching the 0.265 gap and generalized MCC = 0.032 reported above), two permutation analyses (10{,}000 resamples each) were performed to quantify what the observed LOPO statistics imply under a null of uninformative cross-pathogen training.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:445:Second, the mean generalized MCC under random combo selection is $+0.017$ (SD $\approx 0.034$ for a single combo applied to all pathogens; SD $\approx 0.027$ for an independent random combo per pathogen). The observed training-best generalized MCC of $+0.032$ exceeds this null mean but only by approximately $0.4$--$0.6$ SD, yielding a one-sided $p \approx 0.25$--$0.28$. The 0.265 gap is therefore consistent with, but not statistically distinguishable from, a null in which training-based selection provides no cross-pathogen transfer.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:446:This tempering does not invalidate the pathogen-adaptive conclusion: the $\omega^2 = 0.296$ interaction effect, the 9 distinct optimal scoring types across 11 pathogens, and the vaccine-escape cross-validation all speak to pathogen-specific optimality through complementary routes. But it clarifies that LOPO-0/11 and the 0.265 gap, read in isolation, are weaker evidence than the surface reading suggests, and that independent replication on additional pathogens is needed to sharpen the statistical support for cross-pathogen training's inability to transfer.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:476:To test whether the benchmark findings generalize beyond MSA-derived scoring formulas, an independent scoring paradigm was evaluated: the ESM-2 protein language model (650M parameters)~\cite{lin2023esm2}. ESM-2 computes per-position log-likelihood ratios (ESM-LLR) from a single consensus sequence using learned evolutionary representations, requiring no multiple sequence alignment. This provides orthogonal validation of the benchmark framework because the scoring signal originates from a fundamentally different methodology---a deep neural network trained on millions of protein families---rather than from the same MSA used by the other scoring formulas.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:485:The Shapiro-Wilk test on ANOVA residuals rejected normality ($W = 0.974$, $p < 10^{-29}$), and Levene's test rejected homoscedasticity for all factors.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:491:Kruskal-Wallis non-parametric tests confirmed all effects (pathogen: $H = 1{,}120.8$, $p < 10^{-234}$; detection family: $H = 129.1$, $p < 10^{-21}$; scoring: $H = 277.9$, $p < 10^{-47}$), maintaining the reliability of the directional ANOVA conclusions despite these caveats.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:526:\textbf{DMS Validation.}
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:529:For 4 of the 6 DMS pathogens with threshold sensitivity data, Spearman correlations between DMS fitness and the best scoring formula output differed in direction (H3N2: $\rho = 0.191$; HIV-1: $\rho = 0.412$; RSV: $\rho = -0.363$; SARS-CoV-2: $\rho = -0.370$; all $p < 0.002$), confirming that DMS fitness and evolutionary adaptation capture different aspects of mutation impact and validating the 3-layer ground truth design.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:530:Varying the DMS threshold from 10\% to 30\% altered the identity of the best-performing combination in all 4 pathogens (mean best DMS F1: 0.328 $\to$ 0.377 $\to$ 0.479), while the relative rankings of scoring formulas remained stable within the 15\%--25\% range (see Section~\ref{subsec:3layer_gt}), further supporting pathogen-dependent method selection.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:532:To further illustrate the ground-truth dependence, Table~\ref{tab:layer_a_vs_c} compares the best-performing scoring type under Layer~A (convergent evolution) versus Layer~C (DMS fitness) for the 6 pathogens with experimental DMS data.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:536:\caption{Best scoring type under Layer~A vs.\ Layer~C ground truth for 6 DMS pathogens. DMS sources: SARS-CoV-2~\cite{dadonaite2024nature}, H3N2~\cite{lee2018h3n2dms}, HIV-1~\cite{haddox2018hiv1dms}, RSV~\cite{simonich2026rsvdms}, Rabies~\cite{aditham2025rabies}, EV-A71~\cite{bakhache2025eva71}. In all 6 pathogens, the best scoring type differs between the two ground truth layers, confirming their independence.}
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:553:In all 6 pathogens, the best scoring type differs between Layer~A and Layer~C (Table~\ref{tab:layer_a_vs_c}). The Spearman rank correlations between Layer~A and Layer~C scoring rankings are non-significant for 4 of 6 pathogens (SARS-CoV-2: $\rho = -0.13$; H3N2: $\rho = -0.11$; HIV-1: $\rho = 0.27$; EV-A71: $\rho = -0.18$), confirming that Layer~C provides an independent evaluation dimension. RSV ($\rho = 0.85$) and Rabies ($\rho = 0.86$) show strong positive correlations. \textbf{Post-hoc rationalisation check}: the 20 scoring formulas were defined prior to per-pathogen evaluation (Chapter~\ref{ch:mutbench}); the per-pathogen MCC ranking is deterministic given the design and the biological rationale per pathogen is interpretive only. The Layer~A vs.\ Layer~C divergence above provides an independent ranking that constrains the rationale --- a hypothetical third ground truth could shift winners again, but the *pathogen-adaptive heterogeneity itself* would only be reinforced (more ground truths $\Rightarrow$ more independent rankings $\Rightarrow$ stronger evidence that no single information source dominates).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:554:In practice, when Layer~A and Layer~C indicate different optimal scoring types, the choice depends on the research objective: Layer~A rankings should be prioritized for immune evasion surveillance, while Layer~C rankings are more appropriate for functional impact assessment such as DMS-guided drug target prioritization.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:560:The cross-pathogen benchmark supports pathogen-adaptive method selection through two primary analyses (scoring~$\times$~pathogen $\omega^2$ interaction and vaccine-escape cross-validation) plus two null-consistent corroborations (LOPO 0/11 and Friedman). The four lenses re-parameterize the same dataset and are not independent replications.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:565:\item \textbf{Generalization failure}: LOPO cross-validation yielded 0/11 combination matches with a mean generalization MCC of 0.032. The best combination selected from training pathogens does not generalize to new pathogens.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:572:\subsection{Subgroup Analysis: DMS-Available vs DMS-Unavailable Pathogens}
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:575:Six of the 11 pathogens (SARS-CoV-2, H3N2, HIV-1, RSV, Rabies, EV-A71) have DMS-based Layer~C ground truth while five (Dengue, Norovirus, Influenza~B, MERS, HCV) have only Layer~A. A legitimate concern is whether the benchmark systematically under-performs on DMS-unavailable pathogens---if so, the main findings could reflect ground-truth quality rather than biological signal.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:577:Table~\ref{tab:dms_subgroup} reports per-pathogen best MCC (across the 780 scoring--detection combinations) and subgroup means. The DMS-available subgroup's best-per-pathogen MCC averages 0.287 (range 0.196--0.534); the DMS-unavailable subgroup averages 0.407 (range 0.196--0.660). A Mann--Whitney $U$ test on these two best-MCC sets yields $U = 10$, $p = 0.43$ (two-sided), indicating no statistically significant difference in achievable performance between subgroups at the given sample sizes.

chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:608:The DMS-unavailable subgroup is \emph{not} systematically worse; if anything, its best-MCC mean is slightly higher, which argues against the hypothesis that Layer~A alone is a weaker ground truth than Layer~A+C. Two mechanisms likely explain the higher values in the DMS-unavailable group: (i)~HCV's Layer~A is defined by hypervariable-region boundaries rather than point positions, which inflates detectability; (ii)~Norovirus and Influenza~B have denser Layer~A sets, making true positives more abundant and MCC easier to attain. Conversely, the DMS-available group contains pathogens (RSV, Rabies, EV-A71) with narrow, sparse Layer~A sets that cap the achievable MCC.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:610:\textbf{Interpretation}: the main Stage~2 conclusions (scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction dominance, LOPO non-generalization, Friedman non-significance) are supported by both subgroups. The DMS-unavailable pathogens contribute informative signal despite lacking functional validation, and their inclusion does not bias the interaction finding in a direction favorable to the conclusion. However, a mechanistic interpretation of the best scoring type in the DMS-unavailable subgroup remains one step less grounded than in the DMS-available subgroup, since only the latter can be back-checked against independent experimental fitness data; the DMS-unavailable subgroup's results should be treated as phylogenetic-pattern evidence rather than functional-effect evidence.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:631:\item \textbf{Deep learning-based} (2 features): \textit{esm2\_llr} (ESM-2 protein language model log-likelihood ratio~\cite{lin2023esm2,rives2021biological}, measuring how surprising a mutation is relative to learned evolutionary constraints from 250M protein sequences) and \textit{semantic change} (mean cosine distance between wild-type and mutant ESM-2 embeddings at each position~\cite{hie2021learning}, measuring how much a mutation alters the protein's functional context).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:632:\item \textbf{Structure-based} (2 features): \textit{plddt} (AlphaFold2/ESMFold predicted local distance difference test score~\cite{jumper2021alphafold}, indicating structural confidence and disorder propensity) and \textit{SASA} (relative solvent accessible surface area computed from ESMFold-predicted structures using the Shrake--Rupley algorithm~\cite{shrake1973environment}, measuring surface exposure).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:636:These 10 features were selected from a broader set of 22 candidate information types identified from the literature. Features excluded from the analysis include: weighted contact number (WCN, high correlation with SASA, $r > 0.7$), intrinsic disorder prediction (largely redundant with pLDDT $< 50$~\cite{wilson2022alphafold}), co-mutation/mutual information (pairwise rather than per-position feature, incompatible with the univariate per-position analysis framework; additionally $O(L^2)$ computational cost), codon usage bias (weak association with hotspot status), and epitope/glycosylation distance (not uniformly available across all 11 pathogens). The selection criteria were: (1)~independence from existing features, (2)~applicability to all 11 pathogens, and (3)~prior validation in the literature.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:638:Table~\ref{tab:per_feature_auc} and Figure~\ref{fig:feature_auc_heatmap} present the single-feature AUC (area under the ROC curve) for predicting Layer~A membership. Each feature was used as a standalone classifier via threshold sweeping (no model training), providing a direct measure of univariate discriminative power.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:685:To assess feature importance in a multivariate context---where features may interact and provide complementary information---a Random Forest classifier~\cite{breiman2001random} (200 trees, max depth 5, balanced class weights, random state 42) was trained for each pathogen using the 10 features as predictors and Layer~A as the binary label. Feature importances were extracted as mean decrease in impurity (Gini importance), and model performance was evaluated via stratified 5-fold cross-validation AUC.

Benchmark-optimal scoring types also maximize vaccine escape capture, providing independent practical validation of the benchmark rankings. \textit{Note on multiple comparisons and circularity:} Enrichment values represent the best result among $20 \times 39 = 780$ scoring--detection combinations per pathogen; reported $p$-values are nominal Fisher's exact $p$-values. chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:893:For H3N2, FUBAR Bayes factor captures 9 of 29 antigenic drift sites with 9.36-fold enrichment; 8 of those 9 captured positions are already in Layer~A (the audit paragraph below quantifies the resulting novel-only enrichment of 7.19$\times$ with Fisher $p = 0.132$, not significant). The multi-source EqualWeight integration achieves 4.012-fold enrichment ($p = 0.0023$), capturing positions in both antigenic site~A (position~137) and site~B (positions~155, 159, 160, 186, 188), while frequency alone misses the structurally constrained site~B positions.

chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:918:The exclusion reasons fall into four categories: (i)~annotation granularity too coarse (Dengue, Influenza~B, Rabies, Norovirus); (ii)~sample size below the $n \geq 15$ threshold adopted for the three included pathogens (MERS, EV-A71); (iii)~confound with the benchmark's Layer~A set (RSV); and (iv)~mechanism mismatch (HCV: drug-resistance, not immune escape). No pathogen was excluded because of an expectation of low enrichment; the decision was made on data-availability grounds prior to running any enrichment computation. The generalizability of the enrichment finding to the other 8~pathogens therefore remains to be established, and the three validated pathogens should be read as a data-availability convenience sample rather than a balanced subset.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:924:For a typical viral protein of 500 positions, the optimal scoring--detection combination narrows the candidate list to 20--80 positions with 7--9-fold enrichment for escape sites. This transforms hotspot detection from an exhaustive search into a guided investigation, providing a ranked candidate list that directs limited experimental resources toward the most promising positions.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:934:With only 11 reference pathogens (10 available in each LOPO fold), the 13-dimensional pathogen profile space is severely undersampled (dimensions-to-samples ratio $\approx 1.1$), making $k$NN matching unreliable and introducing noise rather than adaptation.
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:956:Stage~1 validated the framework on SARS-CoV-2: MutClust-Hybrid achieved hotspot-score 0.778 on synthetic data, though real GISAID data showed F1 = 0.123 while maintaining biological validity (enrichment $>$ 6.9-fold).
chapters_en/ch4_results.tex:957:Stage~2 extended evaluation to all 11 pathogens (8,580 evaluations), revealing that the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$; 95\% CI [0.195, 0.333]) is the largest modeled variance component (within-cell residual $\omega^2 \approx 0.39$), with LOPO cross-validation yielding 0/11 exact matches and a 0.265 MCC oracle-vs-generalized gap, and Friedman test showing no reliably superior combination ($p = 0.990$).
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:15:It organizes 10 information types into 20 scoring formulas across 6 categories (frequency, MSA-derived, phylogenetic, structural, AI-based, and composite), defines a three-layer ground truth framework (convergent evolution positives as Layer~A, purifying selection negatives as Layer~B, DMS experimental fitness as Layer~C), introduces the hotspot-score composite metric, and presents a two-stage experimental design combining in-depth SARS-CoV-2 analysis (Stage~1) with large-scale comparison across 11 RNA viruses (Stage~2; see Chapter~\ref{ch:results} for detailed statistics).
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:17:\textbf{Contribution 2. Statistical demonstration that the optimal biological information source differs fundamentally across pathogens ($\omega^2_{\text{scoring} \times \text{pathogen}} = 0.296$), with 9 distinct optimal information types across 11 pathogens and no cross-pathogen generalization (LOPO 0/11).}
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:18:Statistical analysis of the large-scale benchmark results across 11 RNA viruses provided, through two primary analyses (the scoring~$\times$~pathogen ANOVA interaction and the vaccine-escape enrichment) and two null-consistent corroborations (LOPO 0/11 and Friedman) on the same 8{,}580-evaluation dataset, consistent evidence that the optimal biological information source is pathogen-dependent.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:21:Third, the Friedman test ($p = 0.990$) showed no reliably superior combination across all pathogens, consistent with pathogen-dependent optimality.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:22:Fourth, Leave-One-Pathogen-Out (LOPO) cross-validation yielded a 0/11 agreement result, showing that the optimal information source for one pathogen does not generalize to others.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:24:\textbf{Contribution 3 (two-part).} \textit{(3a) Multi-source integration infrastructure}: a compact 4-feature core (homoplasy, pLDDT, entropy, frequency) captures $\approx$98\% (97.6\%) of the full 10-feature ensemble performance, and EqualWeight integration achieves a statistically significant 4.012-fold H3N2 enrichment ($p = 0.0023$) where single-feature approaches fail. \textit{(3b) Externally-valid vaccine-escape enrichment, anchored on HIV-1}: the Layer-A-disjoint subset of HIV-1 escape positions (37 of 45) yields a direct novel-only enrichment of $7.16\text{--}8.24\times$ (worst-case Bonferroni-adjusted Fisher $p = 5 \times 10^{-12}$); H3N2's 9.36$\times$ is a self-consistency check (69\% Layer~A overlap); SARS-CoV-2 is exploratory after multiple-comparison correction.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:27:Vaccine-escape enrichment analysis across 3 of 11 pathogens (H3N2, SARS-CoV-2, HIV-1; 2{,}340 evaluations; selected for availability of curated antibody-escape annotations) was audited for circularity against the Layer~A ground truth. \textbf{HIV-1 is the cleanest external validation}: its escape set shares only 8 of 45 positions (18\%) with HIV-1 Layer~A, so the 7.19$\times$ enrichment (Bonferroni-adjusted $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$) primarily reflects detection of positions outside the benchmark's training signal. \textbf{H3N2 should be read as a self-consistency check, not external validation}: 20 of 29 H3N2 escape positions (69\%) are in Layer~A, and on the 9 Layer~A-disjoint (novel) escape positions the top combination's enrichment drops to 7.19$\times$ with Fisher $p = 0.132$ (not significant under any correction), so the headline H3N2 9.36$\times$ predominantly re-measures Layer~A performance under a different label rather than discovering new escape positions. \textbf{SARS-CoV-2 is exploratory only}: the 7.63$\times$ nominal enrichment does not survive Bonferroni correction ($p_{\text{adj}} \to 1$), and 60\% of its escape set overlaps Layer~A. The practical-impact claim of Contribution~3 therefore rests on HIV-1 as the primary external validation, with H3N2 and SARS-CoV-2 contributing self-consistency and exploratory evidence respectively.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:46:Ground truth limited to literature & High & 3-layer GT with DMS validation & Expand to more pathogens \\
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:47:DMS data available for 6/11 pathogens & Medium & Layers A+B for remaining 5 & New DMS experiments (e.g., H5~\cite{dadonaite2024h5}) \\
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:52:GISAID sampling bias & Medium & Weekly temporal stratification & Geographic stratification \\
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:54:GT completeness (false negatives) & Medium & Literature-curated; DMS cross-validation & Expand Layer A with new studies \\
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:57:$\rho$(Layer~A, frequency) pathogen-specific (mean $|\rho|{=}0.12$; HCV 0.33, Inf.B 0.26, Norovirus 0.23) & Medium & Homoplasy/DMS as frequency-independent signals; Ch5 circularity audit & Uniform Layer~A curation protocol across pathogens \\
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:60:LOPO 0/11 expected under random null ($P \approx 0.96$) & Medium & Ch4:432 permutation-null analysis; gap 0.265 as primary evidence & Larger pathogen panel (20--30+) for power \\
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:61:Vaccine-escape available for 3/11 pathogens & Medium & Ch4 Table \ref{tab:escape_availability} availability audit & Curation effort on Dengue/RSV/Rabies escape sets \\
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:70:The full three-layer ground truth (Layers A, B, and C) is available only for the six pathogens with DMS data (SARS-CoV-2, H3N2, HIV-1, RSV, Rabies, EV-A71); the remaining five pathogens are evaluated using only Layers A and B.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:71:Layer~C (DMS functional fitness) is based on published DMS datasets~\cite{dadonaite2023dms}, and for pathogens without available DMS data, functional fitness validation cannot be performed.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:72:Furthermore, in interpreting DMS data, the choice of threshold for defining functionally important positions (top 20\% of mean absolute fitness effect in this study) directly affects the composition of the ground truth, introducing sensitivity to that threshold.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:73:DMS measures in vitro molecular fitness using pseudovirus systems and thus may not fully capture in vivo fitness.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:77:The phylogenetic non-independence of frequency-based scores (Section~\ref{sec:phylo_limits}) and GISAID sampling biases are discussed in Chapter~\ref{ch:discussion}.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:79:A performance gap exists between synthetic and real data due to the sparse distribution of real H-scores, though biological validity is preserved with enrichment ratios above 6.9-fold (see Chapter~\ref{ch:discussion} for detailed analysis).
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:106:6 & Provenance and supplementary-table extensions (DMS preprocessing convention table; CSV-row-to-table-cell provenance manifest; region-overlap LOPO mini-table; Random-Forest CV AUC summary; Bonferroni-survivor median-of-survivors column; Tajima's D / CUSUM / segmentation citation reconciliation) & Existing per-pathogen CSV archive + bib audit & Closes the cycle-12 P2 polish set in one supplementary-table sweep \\
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:119:The proof-of-concept results reported in Section~\ref{sec:phylo_simulation} establish that homoplasy-based scoring captures qualitatively different evolutionary signals from frequency-based H-scores: $\rho = -0.876$ in coalescent simulation, AUC~$= 1.000$ for TreeTime ML ancestral reconstruction ($N = 2{,}000$), and $\rho = -0.107$ on real GISAID sequences ($N = 500$).
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:121:The primary computational bottleneck is TreeTime's $O(N \log N)$ scaling with sequence count, but recent ultrafast alternatives such as UShER~\cite{turakhia2020ultrafast} enable processing of millions of sequences, making this integration feasible at GISAID scale.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:143:These conclusions are bounded by limitations enumerated in Section~\ref{sec:limitations}: the eleven-pathogen scope precludes mixed-effects modeling, a covariate-adjusted (length, positive-rate) variance decomposition has not yet been performed, the LOPO 0/11 result is null-consistent under random-combination permutation, the Layer~A construction is partly literature-curated, the multi-source enrichment claim is statistically anchored by HIV-1, and head-to-head comparison with concurrent benchmarks (ViroGym~\cite{virogym2026}, EVEREST~v3~\cite{gurev2026everest_v3}) remains future work.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:148:\label{sec:code_availability}
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:150:The source code of the MutBench framework, benchmark scripts, ground truth definitions for 11 pathogens, and configuration files necessary for reproducing all experiments will be made available at the GitHub repository (\url{https://github.com/hwijun/mutbench}).
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:151:During the review period, the source code is available to committee members upon request. All detection method implementations, ground truth definitions, and evaluation scripts are organized as a reproducible pipeline with configuration files specifying exact parameters for each experiment.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:157:All stochastic processes (bootstrap resampling, subsampling) used a fixed random seed (42) for reproducibility.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:158:Pathogen sequence data were collected from NCBI GenBank, and SARS-CoV-2 DMS data were obtained from the original data provided by Dadonaite et al.~\cite{dadonaite2023dms, dadonaite2024nature}.
chapters_en/ch6_conclusion.tex:159:GISAID sequence data were accessed under the GISAID Data Access Agreement. The benchmark framework does not redistribute raw GISAID sequences; instead, computed H-scores and detection results are provided.

   221	This framework has been formalized in the machine learning community through meta-learning~\cite{kerschke2019algorithm,bischl2016aslib} and automated algorithm selection (AutoML)~\cite{feurer2015automl,kotthoff2016algorithm}, where the goal is to automatically select the best-performing model or pipeline configuration for a given dataset.
   222	The parallel to MutBench is direct: just as AutoML selects the optimal machine learning pipeline based on dataset characteristics, MutBench's pathogen-to-scoring recommendation table selects the optimal scoring--detection combination based on pathogen characteristics.
   223	However, the algorithm selection framework has not previously been applied to viral genomics, where the ``problem instances'' are pathogens with diverse evolutionary characteristics (genome size, mutation rate, population structure, selective pressure regime) and the ``algorithms'' are scoring--detection pipelines.
   224	
   225	The benchmarking methodology adopted in this dissertation follows established principles from computational biology.
   226	Weber et al.~\cite{weber2019benchmarking} proposed guidelines for neutral benchmarking, articulating three core requirements: (1)~\textit{independent evaluation}, where the benchmark designer is distinct from the method developers; (2)~\textit{multiple metrics}, to capture different aspects of performance and avoid optimization for a single criterion; and (3)~\textit{controlled experimental design}, ensuring that all methods are evaluated on identical data under identical conditions. Mangul et al.~\cite{mangul2019systematic} extended these principles to a community-wide audit of omics computational tools, documenting systematic disparities in tool reliability that motivated the present study's emphasis on multi-pathogen rather than single-pathogen evaluation.
   227	Boulesteix et al.~\cite{boulesteix2017towards} further emphasized the importance of avoiding ``self-assessment bias'' where method developers evaluate their own methods on self-selected datasets, which systematically inflates reported performance.
   228	MutBench adheres to these principles by evaluating all methods---including the author's own MutClust---under identical conditions with independent ground truth, using a composite metric (hotspot-score) that balances precision, recall, and specificity.
   229	
   230	\subsection{Benchmarking Gap in Viral Hotspot Detection}
   231	\label{subsec:bg_benchmarking_gap}
   232	
   233	The absence of benchmark studies for hotspot detection methods in viral genomics stands in contrast to cancer genomics, where Bailey et al.~\cite{bailey2018comprehensive} conducted a comprehensive PanCancer analysis applying 26 computational tools to 9,423 tumor exomes under uniform conditions, producing a widely used catalog of cancer driver genes.
   234	No analogous \emph{detection-task} benchmark exists for viral mutation hotspots: while several recent fitness-regression benchmarks now span comparable virus panels, the region-level hotspot-detection task itself remains unstandardized---detection methods are evaluated using ad hoc validation against small sets of known functional mutations, without standardized datasets, metrics, or ground truth definitions.
   235	Related efforts in adjacent domains include:
   236	(1)~ProteinGym~\cite{notin2023proteingym,notin2025proteingym_v13}, which benchmarks variant effect predictors using 217 DMS assays and 90+ baseline models (as of v1.3) but addresses a per-residue fitness-regression task rather than hotspot region detection;
   237	(1b)~\textbf{ViroGym}~\cite{virogym2026} (Mar 2026), which benchmarks PLM and alignment-based scorers across 13 viruses, 79 DMS assays, 552{,}937 sequences, and 7 phenotypic categories including immune escape---larger virus count than MutBench, but focused on per-variant fitness rather than per-region detection;
   238	(2)~ConDor~\cite{morel2024condor}, which detects convergent mutations across phylogenies but is a single tool rather than a benchmark framework;
   239	(3)~Pons et al.~\cite{pons2020computational}, who reviewed 40+ cancer hotspot detection methods but produced a descriptive survey without a unified benchmark, and cancer-specific models do not transfer to viral evolutionary dynamics;
   240	and (4)~individual SARS-CoV-2 studies using entropy~\cite{harvey2021tracking} or clustering that validate against small variant sets without standardized ground truth.
   241	Among the 35+ mutation clustering tools catalogued in the computational oncology literature~\cite{pons2020computational}, none was designed for or validated on viral population-level mutation data. Cancer hotspot tools (OncodriveCLUSTL, HotMAPS, MutSpot) require tumor cohort somatic mutation calls and human-genome-specific background models (trinucleotide signatures, replication timing). Phylogenetic selection tools (MEME, FUBAR, FEL) detect per-codon dN/dS signals but do not perform spatial clustering of hotspot regions. The only virus-specific hotspot clustering tool is MutClust~\cite{youn2025mutclust}, validated on a single pathogen (SARS-CoV-2). This gap---the absence of systematic multi-pathogen hotspot detection benchmarking---is what MutBench addresses.
   242	Thus, a systematic benchmark with multi-source ground truth, composite evaluation metrics, and cross-pathogen validation remains absent for viral hotspot detection.
   243	
   244	\subsubsection*{Variant Effect Prediction Benchmarks}
   245	
   246	Recent years have seen significant progress in benchmarking variant effect prediction (VEP) methods on proteins. ProteinGym~\cite{notin2023proteingym} established a large-scale benchmark comprising 217 DMS assays and 2.7 million substitution variants, primarily for human and model organism proteins. EVE~\cite{frazer2021eve}, a Bayesian VAE trained on evolutionary sequences, demonstrated that unsupervised generative models can predict disease-associated variants without clinical labels. EVEscape~\cite{thadani2023evescape} extended this framework to viral immune escape prediction by combining EVE fitness scores with structural accessibility and physicochemical dissimilarity, successfully forecasting SARS-CoV-2 Omicron escape mutations from pre-pandemic data.
   247	
   248	Most recently, EVEREST~\cite{gurev2025everest,gurev2026everest_v3} specifically benchmarked VEP methods across WHO priority viruses; the v3 expansion (Jan 2026) covers 45 viral DMS datasets, 31 forecasting clades across 4 viruses, and reliability assessment across 40 WHO priority RNA viruses spanning 16 viral families. EVEREST finds that protein language models substantially underperform alignment-based approaches on viral proteins, that reliability fails for over half of the WHO-40 panel (especially surface glycoproteins), and that prediction reliability varies dramatically across pathogens---a finding that independently corroborates the LOPO 0/11 non-transferability reported in MutBench Chapter~\ref{ch:results}.
   249	The PLANT framework~\cite{plant2025antigenic} and Shah et al.~\cite{shah2024h3n2ml} provide PLM-based and ML-based H3N2 antigenic cartography that explicitly competes with WHO vaccine-strain selection, building on the foundational antigenic-cartography paradigm of Smith et al.~\cite{smith2004antigenic}; MutBench's H3N2 self-consistency check (Section~\ref{sec:cross_validation_escape}) is positioned as a detection-side complement to these prediction-side cartographies, not as a competitor.
   250	A particularly relevant finding from EVEREST is that the performance gap between methods varies by viral family: alignment-based methods such as EVE consistently outperform PLMs across most viral proteins, but the magnitude of this advantage differs substantially between, for example, influenza HA and SARS-CoV-2 Spike.
   251	This pathogen-dependent performance variation parallels the central finding of MutBench (Chapter~\ref{ch:results}).
   252	AlphaMissense~\cite{cheng2023alphamissense} demonstrated proteome-wide variant classification using an AlphaFold-derived architecture, though its focus on human proteins limits direct viral applicability.
   253	
   254	MutBench's unique contribution is the \textit{scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction analysis}: while EVEREST establishes that method performance varies across viruses, MutBench quantifies this interaction through three-way ANOVA ($\omega^2 = 0.296$) and demonstrates that the choice of \textit{biological information source} (not just the computational method) is the dominant performance factor. This finding---that the optimal information source is pathogen-dependent within the 20-type/39-variant design, with the interaction as the largest modeled variance component---has no counterpart in EVEREST or ProteinGym, which treat the scoring/feature set as fixed.
   255	Specifically, MutBench provides three capabilities absent in EVEREST and other VEP benchmarks:
   256	(1)~quantification of the scoring--pathogen interaction through three-way ANOVA, revealing that the scoring $\times$ pathogen interaction ($\omega^2 = 0.296$; 95\% CI [0.195, 0.333]) is the largest modeled variance component (within-cell residual $\omega^2 \approx 0.39$);
   257	(2)~cross-validation via vaccine escape enrichment for the 3 of 11 pathogens with curated escape annotations, with HIV-1 (7.19$\times$, Bonferroni-corrected $p = 2.5 \times 10^{-16}$; escape set 82\% disjoint from Layer~A) as the primary external anchor and H3N2 9.36$\times$ reported as a self-consistency check given 69\% Layer~A overlap (circularity audit in Table~\ref{tab:vaccine_escape_stage3});
   258	and (3)~a concrete pathogen-to-scoring recommendation table enabling application to new pathogens without requiring DMS experimental data.
   259	Furthermore, MutBench introduces the vaccine escape cross-validation paradigm with a per-pathogen circularity audit: HIV-1 provides the cleanest external validation, while H3N2 and SARS-CoV-2 contribute self-consistency and exploratory evidence respectively---a distinction absent from EVEREST or ProteinGym.
   260	Table~\ref{tab:benchmark_comparison} summarizes the key differences between MutBench and these related benchmarks.
   261

   291	\vspace{1em}
   292	\noindent\textbf{Chapter Summary.}
   293	This chapter has reviewed the two bodies of prior work that directly inform MutBench.
   294	Section~\ref{sec:bg_hotspot} surveyed viral mutation hotspot detection methods---from frequency-based and entropy-based scoring through density-based clustering to protein language models and selection-based approaches---and identified a critical benchmarking gap: no standardized framework exists for evaluating and comparing these methods across multiple pathogens with independent ground truth.
   295	The only virus-specific hotspot detection tool, MutClust~\cite{youn2025mutclust}, relies on a single pathogen, single information type (H-score), and self-referential validation, leaving open the question of how different scoring approaches and detection algorithms compare across diverse viral pathogens.
   296	Together, these gaps motivate the design of MutBench as a systematic, multi-pathogen benchmark with three-layer ground truth, composite evaluation metrics, and statistical analysis of scoring--pathogen interactions.
   297	The following chapter presents the MutBench framework in detail, including the construction of multi-layer ground truth datasets for 11 pathogens, the benchmark design comprising 20 scoring types across 6 categories and 14 detection method families, and the factorial ANOVA methodology for quantifying scoring--pathogen interactions.

front_en/abstract.tex:4:Detecting mutation hotspots in viral genomes is essential for variant surveillance and vaccine design, yet existing approaches have relied almost exclusively on mutation frequency and Shannon entropy, leaving comparatively unexplored a rich landscape of complementary information sources (phylogenetic selection signals, protein language models, structural features). Concurrent fitness-regression benchmarks (ViroGym, EVEREST~v3, ProteinGym~v1.3) target per-variant prediction; MutBench is the broadest \emph{region-level hotspot-detection} benchmark to date.
chapters_en/ch1_introduction.tex:33:Existing computational approaches for hotspot detection have relied predominantly on two types of information: mutation frequency and Shannon entropy. While these capture the most direct signals of mutational enrichment, they fail to distinguish biologically meaningful hotspots from founder-effect artifacts and cannot leverage the growing wealth of complementary information sources---including phylogenetic selection signals, protein language model predictions, structural features, and deep mutational scanning data. Concurrent benchmarks evaluate per-variant fitness regression on overlapping virus panels (notably ViroGym~\cite{virogym2026}, 13 viruses / 79 DMS / 7 phenotypes; EVEREST~v3~\cite{gurev2026everest_v3}, 45 DMS / 31 forecasting clades / 40 WHO priority viruses; ProteinGym~\cite{notin2023proteingym,notin2025proteingym_v13}, 217 DMS / 90+ baselines), but none has performed a region-level hotspot-detection comparison that systematically decomposes which biological information types are most effective for which pathogens, leaving researchers to default to frequency-based approaches regardless of the virus under study.
chapters_en/ch1_introduction.tex:142:MutBench is the broadest hotspot-detection benchmark to date, complementing concurrent fitness-regression benchmarks (ViroGym~\cite{virogym2026}, EVEREST~v3~\cite{gurev2026everest_v3}, ProteinGym v1.3~\cite{notin2025proteingym_v13}) by targeting region-level detection rather than per-variant fitness, and is designed to answer the question: \emph{which biological information source is most effective for which pathogen?}
